levels.title: Making a Choice with if
levels.description: An if statement lets a program run an instruction only when a question is true. Python checks the question, runs the indented lines if the answer is True, then continues past them.

levels.title: Using if for a One-Way Choice
levels.description: Use a plain if when there is one special action and nothing else is needed when the condition is false. The program simply skips that action and carries on.

levels.title: Choosing Between if and else
levels.description: Use else when the program needs a second action if the if condition is false. Python runs exactly one of the two branches.

levels.title: Checking Several Choices with elif
levels.description: elif means “else if.” It checks another possibility when earlier checks were false. Python stops at the first true choice, so put high or specific thresholds first.

levels.title: Combining Conditions with and and or
levels.description: and means every joined rule must be true. or means at least one rule must be true. These words help describe real requirements clearly.

levels.title: Putting an if Inside Another if
levels.description: A nested if is an if inside another decision. Python checks the outside rule first and reaches the inside rule only if the outer path allows it.

levels.title: Combining Conditions with and, or, and not
levels.description: and requires every part. or accepts either part. not reverses a True/False answer. Parentheses group a rule so it is easier to read.

levels.title: Avoiding Common if Statement Mistakes
levels.description: A single = stores a value; == compares two values. Indentation shows which lines belong to a branch. In an elif chain, a broad rule placed too early can hide a more specific answer.

learning_objectives: Understand what programming is: giving step-by-step instructions to a computer
Learn your very first Python tool: the print() command
Understand WHY we need print() to see anything on screen

lesson.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed for this lesson.
lesson.introduction: Welcome to Python Quest! Imagine you have a friendly helper robot in your room. This robot can move at lightning speed, but it is born with a totally blank mind. It knows nothing on its own! If you say 'make tea', it freezes because it doesn't know what tea is. You must give it clear, step-by-step instructions: 1. Boil water. 2. Put tea bag in mug. 3. Pour water into mug. That is all programming is: writing down simple, numbered steps so the computer knows exactly what to do.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
### In simple words
A program is a list of instructions. Python follows them from top to bottom. `print()` is an instruction that shows something on the screen.

### Try it step by step
1. Write `print` in lowercase.
2. Put `(` after it and `)` at the end.
3. Put the words you want to show inside quotes: `print('Hello')`.
4. Run the program. The screen should show `Hello`.

The quotes mark the words as text. The parentheses show which value belongs to `print()`. Each new `print()` normally starts a new output line.

### More detail
🎯 WHY DO WE USE THE print() COMMAND?
Computers are silent and invisible workers. If a computer does a calculation or runs a task, it keeps the result hidden inside its memory chip. You won't see anything on your monitor! To make the computer show words or numbers on your screen, Python created a special command called `print()`. Think of `print()` as giving your computer a mouth so it can speak to you!

🤖 WHAT PYTHON DOES STEP-BY-STEP:
When Python reads: `print('System Boot')`
1. Python reads the word `print` → It realizes: 'Aha! The human wants me to display something on the screen!'
2. Python opens the parentheses `(` and looks inside.
3. Python spots the quotation marks `'...'` → It understands: 'These are human words to display, NOT code commands to execute!'
4. Python takes the exact text `System Boot` and prints it onto your screen.
5. Python automatically jumps down to a fresh line, ready for your next instruction!

⚠️ CRUCIAL RULE — CAPITALIZATION MATTERS:
Python is case-sensitive. That means lowercase `print` works, but capitalized `Print` or `PRINT` will fail with an error. Always write `print` in all-lowercase letters!

common_mistakes.mistake: Print('Hello')
common_mistakes.why: Python is case-sensitive! It does not recognize capital 'P'. It must be lowercase 'print'.
common_mistakes.fix: print('Hello')

common_mistakes.mistake: print(Hello)
common_mistakes.why: Missing quotes! Without quotation marks, Python thinks Hello is a command rather than plain words.
common_mistakes.fix: print('Hello')

common_mistakes.mistake: print('Hello)
common_mistakes.why: Missing closing quote! You opened a quote at the start, but forgot to close it before the bracket.
common_mistakes.fix: print('Hello')

lesson.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed for this lesson.
lesson.introduction: Why is Python the most popular programming language on Earth? Because it was designed to read like clean, plain English! In older languages like Java or C++, displaying a single message takes 5 to 7 complicated lines of boilerplate code. In Python, it is just one simple command! But to write Python, you need to understand how Python tells the difference between code and words.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
### In simple words
Python code is made of instructions, while text is information that an instruction can use. Quotes tell Python, “these are words.” Without quotes, Python treats names and symbols as instructions or values.

### Try it step by step
`print('Hello')` shows the word Hello. The quote marks do not appear in the output. Single and double quotes both work, as long as the opening and closing marks match.

Python also cares about capital letters in code: write `print`, not `Print`. The words inside quotes can use any capitalization you want.

### More detail
🎯 WHY DO WE USE QUOTATION MARKS '...' ?
Imagine you tell a robot: 'RUN'. Does that mean *run across the room*, or does it mean *say the word 'RUN' out loud*? It's confusing!
To solve this problem, programmers invented quotation marks `'...'`. Quotes act exactly like speech bubbles in a comic book:
• When Python sees quotes `'...'`, it understands: 'These are plain human words to display. Don't try to execute them as code!'
• If you forget quotes like `print(Hello)`, Python thinks Hello is a computer command name. It searches its memory, cannot find any command named Hello, and panics with an error called `NameError`!

🔍 SINGLE QUOTES VS DOUBLE QUOTES:
You can use single quotes `'Python'` or double quotes "Python". Both work 100% identically in Python! Just make sure whatever quote you start with, you close with the same quote.

⚠️ CRUCIAL RULE — CASE SENSITIVITY:
To Python, lowercase and uppercase letters are completely different symbols. `print` works, but `Print` or `PRINT` will crash. Always use lowercase!

terminology.definition: A piece of human text wrapped in quotation marks ('...' or "...").
Treating uppercase and lowercase letters as completely different symbols (print is NOT the same as Print).
An error that happens when you write a word without quotes that Python does not recognize.

lesson.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed for this lesson.
lesson.introduction: When you write code, you are not just writing for the computer—you are also writing for other humans and for future you! What if you want to leave a note in your code explaining what a line does? That is what comments are for.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
### In simple words
A Python file is a saved set of instructions. The Python interpreter reads the file and carries out each instruction in order. You can run a file from a code editor or from a terminal with a command such as `python my_file.py`.

### Try it step by step
1. Save Python instructions in a file ending in `.py`, such as `hello.py`.
2. Open that file in a Python editor, or open a terminal in its folder.
3. Run the file. Python starts at the first instruction and moves downward.
4. If an instruction prints text, that text appears in the output area.

A comment starts with `#`. Python skips the comment; it is a note for people reading the file. Comments do not install Python or run a program.

### More detail
🎯 WHY DO WE USE COMMENTS (#)?
What if you want to write a personal note to yourself inside your code, like 'This line prints player health'? If you write normal words in code, Python tries to run them and crashes. When you put a hash symbol `#` at the start of a line, you turn it into a **comment**. Python completely ignores it! It acts like an invisible sticky note for humans.

🤖 WHAT PYTHON DOES:
Python executes code sequentially: starting at Line 1, proceeding to Line 2, Line 3, and so forth until the end. But whenever Python spots a `#` symbol, it completely skips the rest of that line and does not print anything from it!

terminology.definition: A note written in code for humans to read. Python completely ignores comments during execution.
Processing code line by line from top to bottom in order.
A plain text file containing Python instructions that can be saved and run.

lesson.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed for this lesson.
lesson.introduction: In 1978, computer scientist Brian Kernighan wrote a tutorial that began with printing 'hello, world'. Since then, every programmer begins with this tradition! But computers were also built for calculations. Let us learn how Python handles numbers and math.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
### In simple words
Text and numbers can look similar but mean different things to Python. Quotes make a value into text. A number without quotes can be used in arithmetic.

### Try it step by step
`print('5 + 5')` displays the characters `5 + 5`.
`print(5 + 5)` calculates the sum and displays `10`.

Try changing one number and running the program again. Keep quotes around words such as `Hello`, but leave quotes off numbers you want Python to calculate.

### More detail
🎯 WHY DO NUMBERS HAVE NO QUOTES?
Notice this massive difference:
1. When you put numbers inside quotes: `print('5 + 5')`
   Python sees text. It displays literally: `5 + 5`
2. When you omit quotes: `print(5 + 5)`
   Python performs the calculation! It displays: `10`

Quotes tell Python: 'Treat this as plain letters to display.' Leaving off quotes tells Python: 'Calculate this mathematically!'

🤖 PYTHON'S BASIC MATH SYMBOLS:
• Addition: `+` (e.g. `10 + 5 = 15`)
• Subtraction: `-` (e.g. `20 - 4 = 16`)
• Multiplication: `*` (the asterisk symbol, e.g. `25 * 4 = 100`)
• Division: `/` (forward slash, e.g. `10 / 2 = 5.0`)

terminology.definition: A whole number without a decimal point (e.g. 5, 42, -10).
A number with a decimal point (e.g. 3.14, 0.5).
A symbol that performs an operation, like + for addition or * for multiplication.

# Numbers without quotes are evaluated mathematically by the CPU:

lesson.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed for this lesson.
lesson.introduction: So far, you have printed one piece of text at a time. But what if you want to print a word AND a calculated number together, like 'Score: 100'? In Python, you can print multiple items in a single line simply by separating them with commas!
lesson.detailed_explanation:
### In simple words
`print()` can show several values on one line. Separate the values with commas; Python puts a space between them by default. The `sep` setting changes that space, and `end` changes what print adds after its output.

### Try it step by step
`print('Score:', 10 + 5)` shows `Score: 15`.
`print('A', 'B', sep='-')` shows `A-B`.
`print('Loading', end='... ')` keeps the next print on the same line.

The comma separates values for `print()`. The plus sign joins or calculates values, depending on their types.

### More detail
🎯 WHY DO WE USE COMMAS INSIDE print()?
When you put commas between items inside `print()`, Python prints each item and automatically inserts a single space in between:
`print('Score:', 50 + 50)` → outputs: `Score: 100`

🔍 THE sep PARAMETER (CUSTOM SEPARATORS):
By default, Python puts a space between comma items. If you want to separate them with a hyphen or dash instead, you tell Python: `sep='-'`!
`print('Apple', 'Banana', 'Cherry', sep='-')` → outputs: `Apple-Banana-Cherry`

🔍 THE end PARAMETER (CONTROLLING LINE ENDINGS):
By default, after printing, Python presses Enter and starts the next line. If you want to stay on the same line, you pass `end='... '`!
`print('Loading', end='... ')` → stays on the same line!

terminology.definition: A value passed into a function inside parentheses, separated by commas.
A parameter in print() that specifies what symbol goes between items (default is space).
A parameter in print() that specifies what symbol goes at the end of the line (default is newline).

lesson.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed for this lesson.
lesson.introduction: In programming, any sequence of characters (letters, numbers, spaces, symbols) wrapped in quotes is called a 'string'. Think of beads strung on a necklace. You can combine and manipulate strings in powerful ways.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
### In simple words
A string is text inside matching quotes. The plus sign joins strings together. Python does not add a space for you, so include a space string (`' '`) when you want one.

### Try it step by step
`'Python' + 'Quest'` becomes `PythonQuest`.
`'Python' + ' ' + 'Quest'` becomes `Python Quest`.

You can also put `\n` inside a string to start a new output line. It is a special two-character code in your program that becomes a line break when printed. Keep the whole message inside one matching pair of quotes.

### More detail
🎯 WHY DO WE USE THE PLUS (+) SIGN WITH STRINGS?
When you put a plus sign `+` between two strings, Python glues them together end-to-end. This is called **concatenation**:
`print('Python' + 'Quest')` → outputs: `PythonQuest`

⚠️ CRUCIAL DIFFERENCE:
Notice that `+` does NOT insert a space automatically! If you want a space, you must add it yourself: `'Python' + ' ' + 'Quest'`.
Also: `print('5' + '5')` outputs `55`, because quotes tell Python they are text characters, not numbers!

terminology.definition: A sequence of characters enclosed in quotation marks.
The operation of joining two or more strings end-to-end using the + operator.
A special character combination representing a newline.

lesson.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed for this lesson.
lesson.introduction: Computers were originally designed as calculation engines. In Python, solving math problems is clean and instant.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
### In simple words
Python can calculate with numbers. Use `+` to add, `-` to subtract, `*` to multiply, and `/` to divide. Put a calculation inside `print()` to show its answer.

### Try it step by step
`print(25 * 4)` shows `100`.
Python follows normal math order: multiplication happens before addition. Use parentheses when you want to choose what happens first: `(5 + 3) * 2`.

Do not put quotes around numbers that you want Python to calculate. Quoted numbers are text.

### More detail
🎯 ORDER OF OPERATIONS IN PYTHON:
Python obeys standard order of operations: parentheses first, multiplication and division next, addition and subtraction last.
`print(10 + 5 * 2)` → evaluates `5 * 2 = 10`, then `10 + 10 = 20`!

You can print both descriptive text and calculated results together using commas:
`print('Total:', 25 * 4)` → outputs: `Total: 100`

terminology.definition: A combination of numbers, operators, and variables that Python evaluates to a single value.

lesson.introduction: Good code is self-explanatory, but great code includes helpful documentation for fellow engineers.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
### In simple words
A comment is a note for a person reading your code. Start it with `#`. Python ignores everything from that symbol to the end of the line, so a commented-out instruction will not run.

### Try it step by step
`# show the score` is only a note.
`print(15 * 6)` is an instruction and displays `90`.
To temporarily stop a line from running, put `#` at the beginning of that line. Remove the `#` when you want it to run again.

### More detail
🎯 WHY DO WE USE COMMENTS?
Comments allow you to:
1. Explain what complex code is doing in simple human words.
2. Provide section headers so your file is organized.
3. Temporarily 'comment out' code during testing to prevent bugs without deleting it.

lesson.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed for this lesson.
lesson.introduction: Every human language has grammar rules: spelling, punctuation, and capitalization. In programming, these rules are called syntax.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
### In simple words
Python expects code to follow exact spelling and punctuation rules. A missing quote or parenthesis can stop the program before it runs. Capitalization matters for Python names such as `print`.

### Try it step by step
Before running a line, check that every opening quote has a matching closing quote, every `(` has a `)`, and names such as `print` use the correct lowercase letters.

At the start of a program, write each top-level line from the left edge. Spaces at the start are used for grouping code inside blocks, which you will learn later.

### More detail
🎯 THE 3 MOST COMMON BEGINNER ERRORS AND HOW TO AVOID THEM:
1. Unclosed quotes: `print('Hello)` → You opened `'` but forgot to close it with another `'` before the bracket!
2. Unclosed parenthesis: `print('Hello'` → You opened `(` but forgot to close it with `)` at the end!
3. Accidental leading spaces: In Python, you must not add random spaces at the very start of a line, or Python will raise an `IndentationError`!

terminology.definition: An error raised when code violates the grammar rules of Python.
An error caused by improper leading whitespace or tab characters.

lesson.title: What Are Variables?
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Understand how computers store information in memory (RAM)", "Learn what a variable is and why programmers use them", "Understand variables as labeled containers or name tags referencing data", "Distinguish between a variable name and its stored value"]
lesson.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed.
lesson.introduction: A variable is a name that points to a value. Think of it like a labeled box: the label helps you find what you stored. In `hero_title = 'Python Explorer'`, the name is hero_title, the equals sign stores the value, and the value is text. You can use the name later instead of typing the value again.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
hero_title = 'Python Explorer'
print(hero_title)

The first line stores text under the name hero_title. The second line asks Python to show that value. The screen says Python Explorer. Quotes mark text values; when you want the value from a variable, write its name without quotes.

Another example:
coins = 25
print(coins)

This stores the number 25 and displays it. A variable can hold text, numbers, and other kinds of values.

lesson.title: Creating Variables
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Master creating variables with descriptive, readable names", "Understand how Python allocates memory automatically", "Understand multiple assignments in a single statement"]

lesson.introduction: In Python, create a variable with a name, an equals sign, and a value. Python works out the kind of value for you. You can assign two related variables on one line: `start_x, start_y = 0, 10` stores 0 in start_x and 10 in start_y, in that order.

lesson.title: Variable Naming Rules
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Learn Python's strict rules for legal variable names", "Understand why variable names cannot start with a digit", "Master snake_case naming conventions (PEP 8)", "Identify Python reserved keywords that cannot be used as names"]
lesson.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed.
lesson.introduction: A variable name can use letters, numbers, and underscores, but cannot begin with a number. Names cannot contain spaces, and Python special words cannot be used as names. Uppercase and lowercase are different, so score and Score are separate names. Use underscores between words, like favorite_language.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
favorite_language = 'Python'
first_score = 90
player_name = 'Alex'

These are valid names. Names like 2score, player name, and first-score are invalid because they start with a number or contain a space or hyphen. Python reports a syntax error when it cannot read a name. Choose a clear name and spell it the same way each time.

lesson.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed.
lesson.introduction: A variable can be updated after it is created. The short form `coins += 25` means add 25 to the current value and save the answer back in coins. This is useful for scores, health, and counters that change while a program runs.

lesson.title: Arithmetic Operators
learning_objectives: Recognize the arithmetic symbols
Use // to find the whole-number quotient
Use % to find a remainder
lesson.prerequisites: World 3: Understanding int() and float()
lesson.introduction: Python can do arithmetic with numbers. The main symbols are `+` add, `-` subtract, `*` multiply, `/` divide, `//` divide into whole groups, `%` find what is left over, and `**` raise a number to a power. Use the symbol that matches the calculation you need.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
Complete example:
a = 17
b = 5
print(a + b)
print(a // b)
print(a % b)

The answers are 22, 3, and 2. `17 // 5` asks how many full groups of 5 fit in 17. Three groups fit. `17 % 5` asks what remains, which is 2.

More examples: `6 * 4` gives 24, `8 / 2` gives 4.0, and `2 ** 3` gives 8. Division with / can produce a decimal. Floor division // gives the whole-number quotient.

terminology.definition: A symbol that tells Python what calculation to do.

lesson.title: Assignment Operators
learning_objectives: Use +=, -=, and *= to update a variable
Understand that each step saves a new value
Follow updates in the order they happen
lesson.prerequisites: World 3: Arithmetic Operators
lesson.introduction: An assignment operator updates a variable and saves the new value. For example, `score += 5` means add 5 to score and keep the answer in score. This is a shorter way to write `score = score + 5`. Python has similar shortcuts for subtracting, multiplying, and dividing.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
Complete example:
score = 10
score += 5
score *= 2
print(score)

First score is 10. `score += 5` changes it to 15. `score *= 2` changes the current 15 to 30. The output is 30. Each shortcut uses the current value, does the calculation, and stores the answer back in the same variable.

Other shortcuts include `-=`, `/=`, `//=`, `%=`, and `**=`. The order matters because every step updates the value used by the next step.

terminology.definition: Storing a value in a variable.
A shortcut that calculates and updates the same variable.
The value stored in the variable right now.

lesson.title: Comparison Operators
learning_objectives: Use comparison symbols to ask questions about values
Tell == apart from =
Understand that comparisons give True or False
lesson.prerequisites: World 3: Assignment Operators
lesson.introduction: A comparison checks how two values relate and gives the answer `True` or `False`. Use `==` to check if values are equal, `!=` for not equal, and `<`, `>`, `<=`, or `>=` to compare size. A single `=` stores a value; two equals signs `==` ask a question.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
Complete example:
score = 75
print(score >= 50)
print(score == 100)

The first comparison asks whether 75 is at least 50, so Python prints True. The second asks whether 75 equals 100, so it prints False.

You can chain comparisons to check a range: `10 <= number <= 50` means number is at least 10 and at most 50. The endpoints are included. A comparison does not change the values; it gives a True or False answer.

terminology.definition: A check that asks how values relate.
Checks whether two values are the same.

lesson.title: Logical Operators
learning_objectives: Use and when both conditions must be true
Use or when either condition is enough
Use not to reverse True and False
lesson.prerequisites: World 3: Comparison Operators
lesson.introduction: Sometimes a program makes a decision using more than one yes-or-no answer. `and` means both checks must be True. `or` means at least one check must be True. `not` flips an answer: True becomes False, and False becomes True.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
Complete example:
age = 20
has_ticket = True
allowed = age >= 18 and has_ticket
print(allowed)

The person is at least 18, so the first check is True. They also have a ticket, so the second check is True. With `and`, both must be True; allowed becomes True.

For `or`, one True answer is enough: `has_ticket or is_vip`. For `not`, `not is_banned` is True when is_banned is False. Use parentheses to make a longer decision easier to read.

terminology.definition: True only when both sides are True.
True when at least one side is True.
Reverses a Boolean answer.

lesson.title: Operator Precedence
learning_objectives: Explain why Python follows a calculation order
Use parentheses to choose what happens first
Work through a mixed calculation step by step
lesson.prerequisites: World 3: Logical Operators
lesson.introduction: When a calculation has several operations, Python follows a set order so it gets the same answer every time. Parentheses are done first, then powers, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. Use parentheses when you want to make the order especially clear.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
Compare these calculations:
print(2 + 3 * 4)
print((2 + 3) * 4)

The first answer is 14 because Python multiplies 3 by 4 before adding 2. The second answer is 20 because the parentheses tell Python to add 2 and 3 first.

A useful order to remember is: parentheses, powers (**), multiplication or division (*, /, //, %), then addition or subtraction (+, -). If two operations have the same priority, Python usually works from left to right. Parentheses can make your intention easier to see.

lesson.title: What Are Loops?
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Understand what loops and iteration are in computer programming", "Understand the DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principle", "Recognize the two primary loop types in Python: while and for"]
lesson.prerequisites: World 4: Conditional Statements
lesson.introduction: Imagine being asked to write 'I will write clean Python code' 1,000 times by hand. It would take hours of tedious, mind-numbing effort. But for a computer, repeating a task 1,000 times takes less than a millisecond! Loops are the engine of repetition in programming.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
A loop asks Python to repeat instructions. Without a loop, you might copy the same print line three times. With a loop, write it once and let Python repeat it.

Use a for loop when you know what items to visit or how many turns you want. Use a while loop when you want to keep going until a condition changes. For example, for _ in range(3): means repeat the indented lines three times. The underscore is a name used when we do not need the turn number.

lesson.title: Understanding while Loops
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Master the syntax of the while loop in Python", "Understand loop variables, initialization, and loop incrementers", "Learn how to guarantee loop termination"]
lesson.prerequisites: Level 40: What Are Loops?
lesson.introduction: A `while` loop is like an `if` statement that refuses to leave! When an `if` statement is True, it runs once and finishes. When a `while` loop is True, it runs, goes back to the top, checks the condition again, and repeats as long as the condition stays True.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
Python checks the condition after while before every turn. If it is True, Python runs the indented lines and checks again. If it is False, the loop ends.

A counter is a number that changes each turn. Give it a starting value, check it in the while line, and update it inside the loop. For example, start at 3, print the number, and subtract 1. It prints 3, 2, and 1. At 0, count > 0 is False, so the loop stops. Without the update, the loop might never stop.

Once it becomes False, the loop stops."}, {"term": "Counter Variable", "definition": "⏱️ Lap Counter: A number (like count += 1) updated on each round so the loop knows when to stop."}]

lesson.title: Understanding for Loops
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Master the syntax of for loops in Python", "Understand how Python iterates directly over items without manual counters", "Iterate over characters in a string"]
lesson.prerequisites: Level 41: Understanding while Loops
lesson.introduction: In many languages, running a loop requires declaring counters, conditions, and incrementers manually. In Python, `for` loops are fundamentally different: they iterate directly over sequences of items! It reads like plain English: 'For each item in this collection, do this.'
lesson.detailed_explanation:
A for loop takes items from a group one at a time. The name after for holds the current item. Python runs the indented lines for that item, then moves to the next one. When there are no more items, the loop ends.

In for fruit in fruits:, fruit first means Apple, then Banana, then Pear. You do not need to move a counter yourself. A word is a group of characters too, so for letter in 'CAT': visits C, A, and T. Use for to do a job for every item in a list or word.

lesson.introduction: What if you want a `for` loop to run 100 times, or count from 10 to 50, or count by 5s? You don't want to type out a list of 100 numbers by hand! In Python, the `range()` function generates arithmetic numeric sequences on demand with incredible memory efficiency.
lesson.detailed_explanation:

lesson.title: break Statement
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Understand how the break keyword works in both for and while loops", "Prematurely terminate a loop when a target item or error condition is encountered", "Recognize that execution jumps immediately to the line following the loop block"]
lesson.prerequisites: Level 43: Understanding range()
lesson.introduction: Imagine searching through a deck of 52 playing cards for the Ace of Spades. Once you find it on card #7, do you keep searching through the remaining 45 cards? Of course not! You stop searching immediately. In Python, `break` lets you bail out of a loop the instant you have found what you need.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
break tells Python to leave a loop right away. Python skips the remaining turns and continues with the first line after the loop.

This is useful when searching. Check items one by one, and as soon as the item you want is found, use break so you do not check the rest. An if line can decide when to stop; the indented break does the stopping. In a nested loop, break leaves only the nearest loop around it.

lesson.title: Nested Loops
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Understand nested loops (loops inside loops)", "Track outer loop cycles vs inner loop cycles", "Calculate coordinates for grids, matrices, and game boards"]
lesson.prerequisites: Level 45: continue Statement
lesson.introduction: How does a digital clock display time? For every 1 hour that passes, the minute hand ticks through 60 minutes! And for every 1 minute, the second hand ticks 60 seconds! That is a nested loop: an inner loop cycling fully for every single tick of an outer loop.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
A nested loop is a loop inside another loop. For every turn of the outside loop, Python runs the inside loop all the way through.

If there are two rows and three columns, the outside loop picks row 0, then row 1. For each row, the inside loop visits columns 0, 1, and 2. That makes six coordinates.

Nested loops can make grids or check every pair of items. Give the two loops different variable names, like row and column, so it is easier to follow.

lesson.title: Infinite Loops and Prevention
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Understand what causes an infinite loop in computer software", "Identify non-terminating while loop conditions", "Use timeout guards, maximum iteration caps, and break conditions to prevent infinite loops"]
lesson.prerequisites: Level 46: Nested Loops
lesson.introduction: Have you ever seen an app freeze, showing a spinning beach ball or 'Not Responding' dialog? In many cases, that freeze is caused by an infinite loop: a loop that never reaches a stopping condition and runs forever, eating 100% of a CPU core.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
An infinite loop never reaches its stopping point. One common cause is forgetting to change the value in a while condition. If count starts at 1 and the code only prints count while count < 4, count stays 1 and the condition stays True forever.

To fix this, change count inside the loop so it moves toward the stopping point. You can also add a maximum turn limit as an extra safety check. Before running a while loop, ask: what changes each turn, and when will the condition become False? If a program gets stuck in a terminal, Ctrl+C usually stops it.
lesson.terminology: [{"term": "Infinite Loop", "definition": "🌀 Runaway Train: A loop whose condition never becomes False, running forever until the computer runs out of memory or you kill it."}, {"term": "Circuit Breaker", "definition": "🛡️ Safety Fuse: A safety counter that automatically breaks out of a while loop after a safe maximum number of laps (e.g. 100)."}]

    print('Running step:', count)
    count += 1

        print('Safety trip activated!')
        break

lesson.title: String Slicing and Indexing
learning_objectives: Read one character using a positive or negative index.
Take a substring with a slice and explain its included start and excluded stop.
Use omitted bounds, steps, and reverse slicing.
Distinguish IndexError from a slice clipped at the end.
lesson.prerequisites: Know that quotes make a string and a variable can store it. Level 49 builds on variables; Level 50 will clean strings.
lesson.introduction: A game receives the code word PYTHON and needs its first and last letters. Direct indexing gets one character; a slice gets a piece such as YTH. Python assigns each character a position so you can ask for exactly what you need.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
A character is one letter, digit, space, or symbol in text. Its index is its position. Python starts indexes at 0: the first character is text[0], the second is text[1]. Negative indexes count backward, with -1 meaning the last character and -2 the one before it.

Use text[index] for exactly one character. If that position does not exist, Python raises IndexError. For example, 'cat'[8] fails. A slice uses text[start:stop]. The start is included and stop is excluded: 'PYTHON'[1:4] includes positions 1, 2, and 3, giving YTH.

Leave start empty to begin at the first character; leave stop empty to continue to the end. Slices that extend past the text are clipped to the available characters, unlike a direct index. A third part is the step: text[start:stop:step]. Step 2 takes every second character; step -1 walks backward, so text[::-1] reverses the string. Slicing returns new text and leaves the original unchanged.

terminology.definition: One letter, digit, space, or symbol in text.
The zero-based position of one character; -1 is the last.
A selected range written with start, stop, and optionally step.
An error from asking for one character at a position that does not exist.

lesson.syntax_breakdown:
text[index]             # one character
text[start:stop]        # start included, stop excluded
text[start:stop:step]
text[:3]                # from the start, before index 3
text[3:]                # from index 3 through the end
text[::2]               # every second character
text[::-1]              # reverse the text

practical_examples.title: Slice, skip, and reverse

print(text[:2])

practical_examples.explanation: The slice stops before its stop index. The step chooses every second character; -1 walks backward.

practical_examples.title: A long slice is clipped safely
practical_examples.code:

practical_examples.explanation: The slice ends at the text's actual end. By contrast, text[99] raises IndexError.

common_mistakes.why: Index 1 means the second character because counting starts at 0.
common_mistakes.fix: Use text[0].

common_mistakes.why: The start is included but the stop is excluded.

common_mistakes.why: A slice clips to the available range; direct indexing requires an existing position.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a slice for a range, and check length before a possibly invalid direct index.

lesson.summary: Indexes select one character: positive indexes start at 0 and negative indexes start at -1 from the end. Slices include start and exclude stop; they can use a step. Direct indexing can raise IndexError, while an overlong slice is clipped.

lesson.title: Essential String Methods
learning_objectives: Call strip(), lower(), upper(), and replace() with method syntax.
Explain that string methods return new strings because strings are immutable.
Save a returned string and chain methods in a useful order.
Use methods to clean typed names or create a simple URL slug.
lesson.prerequisites: Know variables, strings, and print(). Level 49 taught how to select parts of text; this lesson returns cleaned versions of text.
lesson.introduction: People can type a name with extra spaces or different capital letters. A program may need one consistent version before comparing or displaying it. String methods are built-in actions for cleaning and changing text.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
A method is an action called on a value. The dot connects the string to the method, and parentheses call it: name.lower(). strip() removes whitespace from the two ends, not between words. lower() and upper() return text with letters changed to one case. replace(old, new) returns text with matching pieces replaced.

Strings are immutable: a method does not edit the original string in place. It returns a new string. If name is 'SAM', name.lower() produces 'sam', but name remains 'SAM' unless you save the result. Write cleaned = name.strip().lower() when you want to keep the cleaned value.

Chaining runs methods left to right: name.strip().lower() first removes edge whitespace, then lowercases the returned string. Order matters. For a web slug, lowercase the title and replace spaces with hyphens. Use a method when its returned result is useful; otherwise it is easy to call it and accidentally discard the result.

terminology.definition: An action called on a value with dot syntax, such as text.lower().
The new value a method gives back.
Not changeable in place; string methods return new strings.
Calling a method on the result of another method.
Spaces, tabs, or line breaks; strip() removes it from the ends.

lesson.title: Format Text and Numbers
learning_objectives: Insert variables and calculations into text with an f-string.
Use .2f to display two decimal places without changing the stored number.
Align text and numbers with a field width.
Print literal braces by doubling them.
lesson.prerequisites: Know variables, strings, numbers, and basic arithmetic. Level 50 covered string methods; an f-string assembles output from current values.
lesson.introduction: A receipt needs to show an item name and price. Joining text by hand is awkward when values change or need fixed decimal places. An f-string lets Python place values into a sentence and format them for display.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
An f-string begins with f immediately before its quote. Inside braces, Python evaluates an expression and inserts its value. For example, {name} looks up the current value of name; {quantity * price} calculates a total. Without the f prefix, braces are ordinary text.

A colon inside braces starts a format specification. .2f means show a fixed-point number with two digits after the decimal, so 4.5 is displayed as 4.50. This changes the displayed text, not the number stored in the variable.

A width reserves a minimum number of character spaces. In {item:<8}, < means left-align and 8 is the minimum field width. In {price:>7.2f}, > means right-align, 7 is the minimum width, and .2f controls decimals. Long text is not cut off; it may extend beyond its field. For literal braces, double them: f'{{ready}}' displays {ready}.

Use f-strings to build messages, receipts, and reports. Keep the value as a number while calculating; format it when displaying it.

terminology.definition: A string prefixed by f that evaluates expressions inside braces.
Code that Python evaluates to produce a value, such as quantity * price.
Instructions after a colon that control how a value is displayed.
The number of digits shown after a decimal point for fixed-point formatting.
A minimum display width and where the value sits: < left, > right, ^ center.

# :.2f displays two digits after the decimal.
# {item:<8} left-aligns in a minimum width of 8.
# {price:>7.2f} right-aligns in a minimum width of 7.

lesson.title: Introduction to Lists
learning_objectives: Create an ordered list and identify its items.
Read an item by its zero-based index and count items with len().
Use a for loop to visit items one by one.
Change a list item and explain that lists are mutable.
Create and use an empty list.
lesson.prerequisites: Know variables, strings, numbers, and how a for loop repeats. Lists let one variable hold an ordered group of values.
lesson.introduction: A game inventory may contain a map, a potion, and a key. Separate variables become awkward as the inventory grows. A list stores related items together, remembers their order, and lets a program visit or change them.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
A list is an ordered, mutable collection. Write items between square brackets and separate them with commas: items = ['map', 'potion']. Each stored value is an item or element. Order matters because each item has a position.

Use square brackets with an index to read one item. Indexes start at zero, so items[0] is the first item. Negative indexes count backward: items[-1] is the last. len(items) returns the number of items. An empty list is [] and has length 0.

A for loop visits every item in order: for item in items: gives the current item to item on each pass. This works even if the list later grows or shrinks, unlike manually writing several print statements.

Lists are mutable: you can replace an item with items[0] = 'torch'. Lists can also grow and shrink with methods, which Level 53 teaches. Use a list when order matters, repeated values are allowed, or the group will change. A set or dictionary fits different needs.

terminology.definition: An ordered collection written with square brackets.
One value stored in a collection.
A zero-based position used to read or replace one item.
The item count returned by len(list_name).
Able to change after creation.
Visiting items one at a time, often with a for loop.

lesson.syntax_breakdown:
items = ['map', 'potion'] # create a list

items[0] = 'torch'       # replace an item

    print(item)
empty = []               # create an empty list

lesson.title: List Operations and Methods
learning_objectives: Replace a list item by index.
Add one item with append(), several with extend(), or one at a position with insert().
Remove by position with pop() or by value with remove().
Sort in place and explain which methods return a value versus None.
lesson.prerequisites: Know list indexes, loops, and mutability. This lesson explains methods for changing a list; Level 54 covers slices and copies.
lesson.introduction: A game inventory changes as a player finds, uses, or reorganizes items. List methods are ready-made actions for those changes. The right method depends on whether you have one new item, several items, a position, or a value to remove.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
Call a list method with a dot: bag.append('key'). append() adds its argument as one item at the end. extend() visits another collection and adds each of its items. insert(index, item) places one item before the given position. Item assignment, such as bag[0] = 'map', replaces one existing position rather than adding a new one.

pop() removes and returns an item. With no index it removes the last item; pop(0) removes the first. Save the return value if it is needed. remove(value) searches for the first matching value and removes it; if the value is absent, Python raises ValueError.

sort() rearranges the same list in ascending order and returns None. append(), extend(), insert(), remove(), and sort() also change the list and return None. Do not write bag = bag.sort(): that assigns None to bag. Call bag.sort() on its own. sorted(bag) is different: it returns a new sorted list and leaves bag unchanged.

Choose a method based on the job: append one value, extend from several values, insert at a position, pop by position, remove by value, or sort the current list. Check indexes and values before trying to remove them.

Adds its argument as one item at the end.
Adds each item from another iterable.
Removes and returns an item; with no index, removes the last.
Removes the first matching value.
Python's value meaning no result; in-place list methods return None.

items.remove(value)         # remove first matching value
items.sort()                # reorder this list in place

lesson.title: List Slicing and Copying
learning_objectives: Slice a list with included start and excluded stop positions.
Predict what happens when two names refer to the same list.
Make a shallow copy with copy() or [:].
Explain the shallow-copy limit when a list contains mutable inner lists.
lesson.prerequisites: Know list indexing and methods. String slices from Level 49 use the same bounds; this lesson applies slicing to lists and explains copying.
lesson.introduction: A program may need a few middle entries from a list, or a safe working version to edit without changing the saved one. Slicing selects a range. Copying separates the outer list. These tools help avoid surprising changes to shared data.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
A slice uses list[start:stop:step]. The start is included and stop is excluded. items[1:-1] therefore leaves off the first and last values. Leaving out a bound starts at the beginning or continues to the end. A slice creates a new outer list containing the selected items.

Assignment does not copy a list. After second = first, both names refer to the same list. This is aliasing. An append or item assignment through either name is visible through both names.

Use first.copy() or first[:] to make a shallow copy. The outer list is new, so adding or replacing a top-level item in the copy does not change the original outer list. A shallow copy does not copy nested mutable objects. If an item is another list, both outer lists still refer to that same inner list. Changing that inner list is visible through both. Deep copying is a separate tool and is outside this lesson.

Use a slice to select a portion; use a shallow copy for a separate outer list; use simple assignment when shared changes are intended. Always consider whether the items themselves contain mutable objects.

terminology.definition: A selected range; start is included and stop is excluded.
The connection from a variable name to the object it refers to.
Two or more names refer to the same object.
A new outer list whose nested objects are still shared.
Changing an existing object's contents.

lesson.syntax_breakdown:
items[start:stop:step]
items[1:-1]        # omit first and last
second = first     # both names refer to the same list
second = first.copy() # shallow copy
second = first[:]     # another shallow-copy form
# Inner lists are still shared by a shallow copy.

practical_examples.explanation: The slice begins at index 1 and stops before index -1. It returns a new list with blue and green; colors is unchanged.

practical_examples.title: Assignment shares; copy() separates the outer list
practical_examples.code:

practical_examples.explanation: alias shares original, so gold appears in original. copy is a separate outer list, so adding green to it does not change original.

common_mistakes.mistake: Thinking second = first copies a list.
common_mistakes.why: Assignment creates another name for the same object.
common_mistakes.fix: Use first.copy() or first[:] for a shallow copy.

common_mistakes.why: The stop index is excluded.
common_mistakes.fix: Use items[1:4] to include positions 1, 2, and 3.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming copy() duplicates every nested list.
common_mistakes.why: copy() makes a shallow copy and keeps references to inner objects.
common_mistakes.fix: Remember that changing a shared inner list affects both outer lists.

lesson.real_world_apps: A history screen can display only recent actions with a slice. A program can make a copy of a shopping list before proposing edits. Nested records require extra care because a shallow copy still shares inner lists or dictionaries.
lesson.summary: Slices select ranges with an included start and excluded stop. Assignment shares a list. copy() and [:] create shallow copies: the outer list is new, but nested mutable items remain shared.

lesson.title: Introduction to Tuples
learning_objectives: Create a tuple and read values by index.
Explain that a tuple is ordered but its positions cannot be reassigned.
Create a one-item tuple using a trailing comma.
Choose a tuple for a fixed group and a list for a group that changes.

lesson.prerequisites: Know variables, lists, and indexes. A tuple resembles a list but is chosen when its positions should stay fixed.
lesson.introduction: A map coordinate has an x and y value that belong together. If the pair should keep its order and not have one position replaced accidentally, a tuple is a suitable container.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
A tuple is an ordered collection, often written with parentheses and commas: point = (4, 7). Its first value is at index 0 and its second at index 1, like a list. len(point) counts its values.

Tuples are immutable as containers. You can read point[0], but assigning point[0] = 9 raises TypeError. Choose a tuple for a fixed coordinate or color; choose a list when items need to be added, removed, or replaced.

The comma makes a tuple. (5) is the integer 5 in parentheses. (5,) is a one-item tuple. With several values, commas separate the items.

Immutability applies to the tuple's slots, not recursively to every object inside. If a tuple contains a list, that inner list can still be changed. The tuple continues to refer to the same list object.

terminology.definition: An ordered collection whose positions cannot be reassigned after creation.
A container whose stored positions cannot be replaced, added, or removed.
A tuple with one value; its comma is required, as in (5,).
An object whose contents can change, such as a list inside a tuple.

lesson.title: Tuple Packing and Unpacking
learning_objectives: Pack values into a tuple, with or without parentheses.
Unpack values into variables in matching order.
Swap two values with multiple assignment.
Predict the error when value count and target count differ.
Unpack pairs in a for loop.
lesson.prerequisites: Know tuples, variables, and loops. Level 55 introduced fixed ordered groups; this lesson names tuple values as they are assigned.
lesson.introduction: A coordinate may arrive as a pair (4, 7), or a score report may contain a name and score. Instead of repeatedly reading positions, unpacking gives each value a clear variable name in one statement.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
Packing puts several values into one tuple. point = (4, 7) packs two values; point = 4, 7 also works because commas make a tuple.

Unpacking assigns tuple items to targets in order: x, y = point sends the first item to x and the second to y. There must be the same number of targets as values. If the counts differ, Python raises ValueError. Unpacking does not sort or search; it uses the existing order.

Multiple assignment is useful for swapping: left, right = right, left. Python evaluates the right-hand values before assigning them, so neither old value is lost.

A loop can unpack pairs too. In for name, score in records:, each record's first value goes to name and second to score. Use this when every item has the same shape and the order of each pair is meaningful.

terminology.definition: Putting several values together in a tuple.
Assigning tuple values to several variables in order.
A variable on the receiving side of an assignment.
One statement assigning multiple values, including a safe swap.
An error raised when unpacking gets a different number of values than targets.

lesson.title: Introduction to Sets
learning_objectives: Create sets and explain how they remove duplicate values.

lesson.prerequisites: Know lists and duplicates. A set is a collection chosen for uniqueness and membership, not positional access.
lesson.introduction: A game records tags a player has collected, but the same tag can arrive more than once. A list keeps every repeat. A set keeps one copy of each distinct value, so it is useful for unique tags and membership checks.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
A set stores unique hashable values. Braces can create one: tags = {'python', 'game'}. If a value appears twice, the set keeps one copy. Sets have no positional order, so tags[0] is invalid. Use a loop to visit items or sorted(tags) when you need a predictable display.

The in operator asks whether a value is present: 'python' in tags returns True or False. This is a direct way to check whether an item has already been collected.

Use set() for an empty set. Empty braces {} make an empty dictionary. Set elements must be hashable: strings and numbers are common examples. Lists can change, so they cannot be set elements; a tuple of hashable values can be.

Use a list when order or repeated items matter. Use a set when you need distinct values and membership checks. Never rely on the order in which a set prints; sort comparable items when order matters to a person.

terminology.definition: An unordered collection of unique hashable values.
Whether a value is present; test with value in collection.
A value suitable as a stable set element or dictionary key.

lesson.title: Set Operations (Union, Intersection, Difference)
learning_objectives: Use | for union and & for intersection.
Use - for directional difference and ^ for symmetric difference.
Explain which values each operation keeps.
Sort results for predictable display.
lesson.prerequisites: Know that sets keep unique values and have no indexes. Level 57 introduced set creation and membership.
lesson.introduction: Two friends have game items. You may want everything they own, only the shared items, items only one friend owns, or items owned by exactly one friend. Set operations express each question directly.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
Let A = {'red', 'blue'} and B = {'blue', 'green'}. Union, A | B, combines values from either set and keeps each once. Intersection, A & B, keeps only values in both. Difference, A - B, keeps values in A that are not in B. Difference is directional: A - B can differ from B - A.

Symmetric difference, A ^ B, keeps values that appear in one set but not both. In this example, red and green remain; shared blue is excluded. Each operator returns a new set and leaves the original sets unchanged.

Sets do not promise display order. sorted(result) returns a list in a predictable order when values can be compared. Choose by the question: everything means |; shared means &; from the first group only means -; in one group but not both means ^. Reading the operation in plain words prevents confusing difference with symmetric difference.

terminology.definition: All distinct values from either set.
Only values found in both sets.
Values in the left set but not the right; direction matters.
Values in exactly one set, excluding shared values.
Returns an ordered list for predictable display.

lesson.syntax_breakdown:

A & B # intersection: only shared values
A - B # in A, not in B
A ^ B # in one set, not both

lesson.title: Introduction to Dictionaries
learning_objectives: Create a dictionary of key-value pairs and retrieve a value by key.
Add a new pair or update the value under an existing key.
Explain unique keys and the hashable-key requirement.
Predict the result of looking up a missing key with brackets.
Choose a dictionary for labeled information rather than numbered positions.
lesson.prerequisites: Know variables, strings, numbers, and lists. A dictionary connects each value to a meaningful label such as name, level, or score.
lesson.introduction: A student record may contain a name, class, and score. Separate numbered positions are hard to remember. A dictionary labels each value, so code can ask for the score by its key instead of remembering its position.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
A dictionary maps keys to values. Write pairs inside braces: hero = {'name': 'Mia', 'level': 3}. The key 'name' labels Mia; 'level' labels 3. A colon separates key and value, and commas separate pairs.

Use hero['name'] to retrieve Mia. Assignment adds or updates: hero['level'] = 4 changes an existing value; hero['class'] = 'Ranger' creates a new pair. Keys are unique, so assigning to an existing key replaces its old value. Values may repeat.

Keys must be hashable. Strings and numbers are common keys; lists are mutable and cannot be keys. Looking up a missing key with brackets raises KeyError. Level 60 introduces get() for cases where a key may be absent.

Dictionaries preserve insertion order in modern Python, but use them as mappings rather than numbered sequences. A list is better for an ordered group of repeated records; each record can be a dictionary so its fields are labeled.

terminology.definition: A mapping that connects keys to values.

lesson.title: Essential Dictionary Methods
learning_objectives: Use get() to return a fallback for a missing key without changing the dictionary.
Visit keys, values, or key-value pairs with dictionary methods.
Unpack each pair from items() inside a loop.
Use update() and pop() and understand their side effects and return values.
Choose brackets or get() based on whether a key must exist.
lesson.prerequisites: Know how to create, retrieve, and update dictionary entries. Level 59 explained that a missing bracket lookup raises KeyError.
lesson.introduction: A settings screen may need to show a theme even when the user has never chosen one. The program needs a safe fallback. Dictionary methods help with missing keys and with processing many stored labels and values.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
get(key, default) returns the value when a key exists. If it is missing, get() returns the supplied default instead of raising KeyError. With no default it returns None. get() does not add the missing key; assign with brackets when you want to create it.

keys() gives the keys, values() gives the values, and items() gives key-value pairs. A loop can unpack those pairs: for subject, score in scores.items():. Each pair's first value goes to subject and the second to score. Iteration follows dictionary insertion order.

update(other) adds new pairs or replaces values for matching keys. It changes the original dictionary and returns None. pop(key) removes a pair and returns its value. You can pass a fallback to pop() for a missing key. Save pop()'s return when it matters; do not assign update()'s return to the dictionary.

Use bracket lookup when the key is required and a missing key is a real problem. Use get() when absence is normal and the program should continue with a useful fallback.

terminology.definition: Returns a present value or a fallback when the key is missing; does not insert the fallback.
Provides key-value pairs for iteration.
Provide the dictionary's keys or values for iteration.
Adds or replaces pairs in place and returns None.
Removes a key and returns its value.

lesson.title: Nested Collections (2D Data & JSON Models)
learning_objectives: Read a cell from a list of lists one level at a time.
Read a field from a dictionary inside a list.

lesson.prerequisites: Know lists, indexes, dictionaries, and keys. A nested collection stores a familiar list or dictionary inside another collection.
lesson.introduction: A game board has rows and columns, while a class roster has records with names and scores. One flat sequence cannot clearly represent all of these layers. Nested collections keep related groups together and let you select one level at a time.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
A nested collection contains another collection as an item. A grid can be a list of lists: grid = [['A', 'B'], ['C', 'D']]. The outer list stores rows; each inner list stores its cells. To get B, Python first evaluates grid[0] and gets ['A', 'B']; then [1] selects B. So grid[0][1] means first row, second cell.

A list of dictionaries stores ordered records. In students[0]['name'], the first bracket selects the first dictionary; the second asks that dictionary for the value under name. Read from the outside inward and keep track of what each expression returns.

Lists are useful for ordered groups; dictionaries label the fields in a record. Nested structures combine those jobs. JSON is a text format for exchanging data. It resembles Python lists and dictionaries, but JSON text is not itself a Python dictionary; it must be parsed into Python values before normal dictionary access.

An inner list is still mutable. Changing it changes the object stored inside the outer list. When a nested expression looks confusing, evaluate one bracket at a time and name the intermediate row or record.

terminology.definition: A collection stored inside another collection.
A list of row lists; one index selects a row and another selects a cell.
Related fields, often stored in a dictionary under clear keys.

lesson.title: Iterating Over Collections (enumerate & zip)
learning_objectives: Use a for loop to visit each item.
Use enumerate() to receive both an item and its count.
Set enumerate()'s starting count with start=.
Use zip() to pair values at matching positions and unpack the pair.
Explain that zip() stops at the shortest input and does not check equal lengths.
lesson.prerequisites: Know lists, for loops, and tuple unpacking. Level 56 explained how two values can be assigned to two loop variables.
lesson.introduction: A menu needs numbers beside each choice, and a report needs to match each person with a score. A loop can visit items, but manual counters and indexes can be easy to misalign. enumerate() and zip() provide the needed pairs as the loop runs.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
A for loop visits items one by one. enumerate(items) pairs each item with a count: by default the first count is 0. Use enumerate(items, start=1) when people expect numbering to begin at 1. The loop can unpack each pair: for number, choice in enumerate(choices, start=1):.

zip(names, scores) pairs values by position: first name with first score, second with second, and so on. for name, score in zip(names, scores): unpacks each pair. The lists must be in corresponding order for the pairing to make sense.

zip() stops when the shortest input runs out. If there are three names and two scores, it makes two pairs and leaves the extra name unused. It does not warn or raise an error. Compare lengths first if equal counts are required.

Use enumerate when one collection needs a count. Use zip when separate collections contain matching values in the same order. If the order is not trustworthy, keep related values together in records instead of pairing by position.

terminology.definition: Repeating an action once for each item in a collection.
Pairs every item with a count; the default count begins at 0.
Pairs items from several iterables by matching positions.
Assigning the parts of each pair to separate loop variables.
Keeping related values at matching positions in separate collections.

scores = [92, 85]
for name, score in zip(names, scores):
    print(f'{name}: {score}')
practical_examples.explanation: There are three names but two scores. zip creates two pairs and stops; it does not include Bo or report the mismatch.

line_by_line.explanation: enumerate returns a count beginning at 1 and the current item; unpack the pair into number and choice.

common_mistakes.mistake: Expecting enumerate(items) to begin at 1.
common_mistakes.why: The default start is 0.
common_mistakes.fix: Use enumerate(items, start=1) for human-facing numbering.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pairing lists that are in different orders.
common_mistakes.why: zip matches positions and cannot know which values belong together.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep both lists aligned or store each record together.

common_mistakes.mistake: Expecting zip() to reject lists of different lengths.
common_mistakes.why: zip stops quietly at the shortest iterable.
common_mistakes.fix: Compare lengths first when matching counts are required.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using pair[0] and pair[1] everywhere in the loop.
common_mistakes.why: The code hides what each value means.
common_mistakes.fix: Unpack with for name, score in zip(names, scores).

lesson.real_world_apps: enumerate() numbers menu options, search results, and report rows. zip() matches names and scores or products and prices when both collections are in the same order.
lesson.summary: enumerate() adds a count to each item; its default starts at 0. zip() pairs items at matching positions. Unpack pairs into clear loop variables. zip() stops at the shortest input and does not validate lengths.

lesson.title: World 6 Examination & Capstone: Student Records Management System
learning_objectives: Design a student record as a dictionary with meaningful keys.
Store many records in a list and retrieve nested values from the outside inward.
Update a student's score and calculate an average using sum() and len().
Collect unique course names in a set and sort them for display.
Use enumerate() and f-strings to print a numbered report.
Explain why each collection fits its job and distinguish Python data from JSON text.
lesson.prerequisites: This project uses strings, lists, tuples, sets, dictionaries, nested access, loops, enumerate(), and f-strings from World 6, plus basic addition, division, sum(), and len(). The steps recap each tool as it appears.
lesson.introduction: A teacher wants a small program that stores several student records, adds a score, finds all courses taught, and prints a readable report. Different parts of the information have different needs: students stay in order, each student's fields need labels, scores and courses can contain several values, and course names should be unique in the final catalog. This capstone combines the right collection for each job.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
Plan the shape of the data first. One student record is a dictionary: the key 'name' labels the student's name, 'scores' labels a list of scores, and 'courses' labels a list of course names. The outer students list stores several records in order. Each structure has one job: a list keeps an ordered group; a dictionary makes fields readable by name; a set removes duplicate course names.

Stage 1: Read one nested value. students[0] selects the first dictionary from the outer list. students[0]['name'] then selects that dictionary's name. Read one bracket at a time to avoid mixing up the outer list index and inner dictionary key.

Stage 2: Update a record. students[0]['scores'] reaches Mia's score list. append(96) changes that list by adding one score. The record is a dictionary, and its scores value is a list, so the nested access follows those two layers.

Stage 3: Collect unique courses. set() creates an empty set. The nested loops visit each student and then each course in that student's course list. add(course) stores each course; if Art appears again, the set still keeps one Art. A set has no display order, so sorted(all_courses) creates a predictable ordered list for the report.

Stage 4: Calculate and report. enumerate(students, start=1) pairs each student with a count for the printed report. sum(scores) adds the numbers; len(scores) counts them; dividing the total by the count gives the average. The program stores intermediate values in names so the final f-string stays readable. The .1f format displays one digit after the decimal; it does not change the average variable. join() combines course names with comma-space separators.

The complete program stays in memory. It does not save a file or connect to a database. The dictionaries and lists are Python objects, not JSON text. A real student system would need input checks, saved storage, privacy protection, and access controls; those topics are beyond World 6. The small program here teaches how collections can fit together to solve one coherent problem.

terminology.definition: A dictionary describing one student with labeled fields.
A list or dictionary stored inside another collection.
A course name included once even if several students take it.
The sum of scores divided by the number of scores.
Readable output assembled from stored records.
A text format for exchanging structured data; it is different from the live Python dictionaries used here.

practical_examples.title: Complete project: Student Records Management System
practical_examples.code:
students = [
    {'name': 'Mia', 'scores': [88, 92], 'courses': ['Python', 'Art']},
    {'name': 'Kai', 'scores': [75, 85], 'courses': ['Art', 'Science']}
]

# Add a new score to Mia's existing scores list.
students[0]['scores'].append(96)

# Gather course names; the set keeps each course only once.
all_courses = set()
for student in students:
    for course in student['courses']:
        all_courses.add(course)

print('Unique courses:', sorted(all_courses))
print('Student report:')
for number, student in enumerate(students, start=1):
    scores = student['scores']
    average = sum(scores) / len(scores)
    name = student['name']
    course_text = ', '.join(student['courses'])
    print(f'{number}. {name} - Average: {average:.1f}')
    print(f'   Courses: {course_text}')
practical_examples.explanation: The outer list keeps students ordered. Each dictionary labels one record's fields. Scores and courses are inner lists because one student can have several. The first nested assignment adds a score to Mia. The nested loops gather each course into a set, removing repeats. sorted() makes course output predictable. The final loop numbers each student, calculates the average, joins course names, and formats each line.

lesson.real_world_apps: A small gradebook, club roster, or course tracker can store people as a list of records. Each record's dictionary labels fields; inner lists store multiple scores or courses; a set can build a unique course catalog. A real school system would also need safe storage and privacy controls.
lesson.summary: A list keeps student records in order; dictionaries label each record; inner lists hold repeated scores and courses; a set removes duplicate course names. enumerate() numbers the report, sum()/len() calculate averages, and f-strings format readable output.

lesson.title: List, Dict, and Set Comprehensions
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Construct list comprehensions with transformation expressions and filtering conditions", "Build dictionary comprehensions {k: v for ...} and set comprehensions {x for ...}", "Understand how comprehensions run faster in C-bytecode than equivalent append loops"]
lesson.prerequisites: World 10: Object-Oriented Programming
lesson.introduction: In Python, creating a new list by transforming or filtering an existing one using an explicit 5-line `for` loop with `.append()` is considered unpythonic. Python provides comprehensions — a concise, declarative syntax that expresses the entire operation in a single elegant line that runs faster in C-bytecode.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
List Comprehensions (Turbo Builders):

1. `⚡ The 1-Line Superpower`: Turns 4 lines of `squares = []; for ... append()` into 1 elegant, high-speed line!
2. `🏭 Transform on Left`: What you want in the new list goes first: `[name.upper() for name in names]`.
3. `🧹 Filter on Right`: Append `if x > 0` at the very end to filter out negative numbers or junk.

lesson.title: Iterators and the Iteration Protocol
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Distinguish between an Iterable and an Iterator", "Manually advance iterators using iter() and next()", "Understand how for loops intercept StopIteration behind the scenes"]
lesson.prerequisites: Level 106: List, Dict, and Set Comprehensions
lesson.introduction: When you write `for item in sequence:`, what is Python actually doing behind the scenes? It doesn't use a numeric index counter! Python uses the universal Iteration Protocol: converting the collection into an Iterator and pulling items one by one with `next()`.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
Iterators and the Iteration Protocol:

1. `🍬 The Pez Dispenser Analogy`: Instead of dumping 1,000,000 candies on the floor, an iterator keeps them in a stack and hands you one candy at a time when you press `next()`.
2. `🔄 How Loops Work Behind the Scenes`: Every time you write `for item in items:`, Python secretly calls `iter()` and `next()` under the hood!
3. `🛑 StopIteration`: Python's silent signal that says 'we reached the end of the collection!'.

lesson.title: Generators and the yield Keyword
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Define generator functions using the yield keyword", "Understand execution pausing and resumption in generators", "Leverage lazy evaluation to process massive data with near-zero memory footprint"]
lesson.prerequisites: Level 107: Iterators and the Iteration Protocol
lesson.introduction: What if you need to calculate the first 10,000,000 Fibonacci numbers? Generating a list of 10 million numbers requires gigabytes of RAM and takes seconds to compute before you can even look at the first number. A Generator creates numbers on demand, one at a time, consuming virtually zero memory!
lesson.detailed_explanation:
Generators & The `yield` Keyword:

1. `⏸️ yield vs return`: `return` finishes the function and destroys its state. `yield` pauses the function like a movie, hands you the value, and freezes until you ask for the next one!
2. `🪶 Saving Gigabytes of RAM`: If you generate 100,000,000 rows from a database, a normal list would crash your computer out of memory. A generator yields 1 row at a time with 0 lag!
3. `✨ Lazy Evaluation`: Calculates values ONLY when requested.

lesson.title: Generator Expressions vs List Comprehensions
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Construct generator expressions using parentheses: (x for x in iterable)", "Compare memory usage between eager list comprehensions and lazy generator expressions using sys.getsizeof()", "Pass generator expressions directly into aggregators like sum(), min(), max()"]
lesson.prerequisites: Level 108: Generators and the yield Keyword
lesson.introduction: Did you know that changing square brackets `[]` to parentheses `()` turns a list comprehension into a generator expression? This simple syntax difference can reduce your program's memory consumption from 800 Megabytes down to 100 Bytes!
lesson.detailed_explanation:
Generator Expressions vs List Comprehensions:

1. `[] vs ()`: Square brackets `[]` build a full list in memory right now. Round parentheses `()` build a streaming generator pipeline.
2. `⚡ Huge Sums in 1 Line`: `sum(x for x in range(1000000))` computes the sum without ever creating a giant 1,000,000-item list in RAM!
3. `💡 Rule of Thumb`: If you need to index `[0]` or slice `[:]`, use a list. If you just need to loop through once or sum, use a generator!

lesson.prerequisites: Level 109: Generator Expressions vs List Comprehensions
lesson.introduction: Can a function remember a variable even after the outer function that created it has completely finished running and exited? Yes! In Python, this phenomenon is called a Closure. Closures are the conceptual foundation of decorators.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
Closures & First-Class Functions:

1. `🎫 Functions are Values`: You can do `my_tool = print` and then type `my_tool('Hello')`!
2. `🎒 The Closure Memory Backpack`: Notice how `double(5)` remembers that `factor` was `2`, even though `make_multiplier` already finished 10 minutes ago!
3. `🏗️ Foundation of Decorators`: Closures are the secret engine behind Python decorators.

lesson.title: Function Decorators (@decorator syntax)
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Understand decorators as higher-order functions wrapping target functions", "Use the @decorator syntactic sugar", "Preserve function metadata (name, docstring) using functools.wraps"]
lesson.prerequisites: Level 110: Closures and First-Class Functions
lesson.introduction: What if you need to measure the execution time of 20 different functions, or ensure that only logged-in users can access 15 web routes? Copy-pasting timing or authentication code into every single function creates bloated, unmaintainable code. Decorators let you wrap existing functions with reusable behavior in a single line: `@my_decorator`.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
Function Decorators (`@decorator`):

1. `🎁 The Gift Wrapping Analogy`: You have a toy (the function). A decorator wraps the toy in wrapping paper (extra code before and after) without changing how the toy itself works!
2. `⏱️ Real-World Uses`: Used everywhere in Python for measuring execution speed, checking if a user is logged in, and rate limiting.
3. `🎀 The @ Sugar`: Writing `@announce` above `def launch():` is a clean shortcut for `launch = announce(launch)`.

lesson.introduction: What if you want to configure your decorator — for instance, specifying how many times to retry an API call `@retry(max_attempts=3)` or setting a rate limit `@rate_limit(calls=60)`? Because you are passing arguments to the decorator itself, you need a Decorator Factory.
