lesson.title: Recursion and the Call Stack
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Understand how a function can call itself (Recursion)", "Identify the two mandatory components: Base Case and Recursive Step", "Understand the call stack and prevent RecursionError (Stack Overflow)"]
lesson.prerequisites: Level 112: Decorators with Arguments
lesson.introduction: To understand recursion, you must first understand recursion! In computer science, recursion is an elegant technique where a function solves a problem by breaking it down into smaller instances of the exact same problem until it reaches a trivial baseline.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
Understanding Recursion:

1. `🪞 The Russian Nesting Doll Analogy`: You open a big doll, and inside is a smaller doll, and inside that is an even smaller doll until you reach the tiny solid doll (the Base Case)!
2. `🛑 Base Case is Mandatory`: Without a base case, the function calls itself forever until Python crashes with a `RecursionError`!
3. `🌲 Perfect for Trees & Folders`: Essential for traversing nested folder structures or binary search trees.
lesson.terminology: [{"term": "Recursion", "definition": "🪞 Hall of Mirrors: A function that solves a problem by calling ITSELF with a smaller piece of the problem until it hits a base case."}, {"term": "Base Case", "definition": "🛑 Emergency Stop Sign: The simple condition where the function stops calling itself and returns a direct answer (e.g. if n <= 1: return 1)."}, {"term": "Call Stack", "definition": "🥞 Stack of Pancakes: The memory stack where Python stores each recursive call while waiting for answers from below."}]
lesson.syntax_breakdown:
def countdown_recursive(n):
    # 1. Base Case (Stop Sign):
    if n <= 0:
        print('🚀 BLAST OFF!')
        return
    # 2. Recursive Step (Calling self with n - 1):
    print(n)
    countdown_recursive(n - 1)

lesson.title: Working with APIs and HTTP Requests
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Explain how a client asks a server for something.", "Choose GET, POST, PUT, or DELETE for a requested action.", "Read common HTTP status-code groups."]
lesson.prerequisites: World 11: Advanced Python
lesson.introduction: When you open a page, your browser asks another computer for information. The server sends back the information or a short code explaining what happened.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
A client is the program that asks for something. A server receives the request and sends a reply. A browser is often a client, and the website is often the server.

The HTTP method says what the client wants: GET reads information, POST sends new information, PUT updates information, and DELETE removes information.

The status code tells how the request went. Codes 200–299 mean success. Codes 400–499 mean the request has a problem, such as a missing page. Codes 500–599 mean the server has a problem. This level practices sorting those replies with Python choices; the example does not contact the internet.

lesson.introduction: A web service often sends its answer as JSON text. Python can turn that text into dictionaries and lists so your program can use the values.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
An API lets one program ask another program for information or an action. The reply has a status code and a response body. The body is the returned data.

JSON is a common text format for that data. It can contain names, values, lists, and nested objects. json.loads(text) reads the text and creates normal Python dictionaries, lists, numbers, and strings.

Check the status before reading fields such as title or data. A successful reply might include those fields; an error reply might contain something different. Our examples use saved sample replies, so they practice handling responses without making a real internet request.

lesson.learning_objectives: ["Tell database tables, rows, and columns apart.", "Explain why each row needs a primary key.", "Recognize SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE."]
lesson.prerequisites: Level 117: Consuming REST APIs in Python
lesson.introduction: A database table is like a classroom roster. Each row is one person, and each column is one detail such as a name or score.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
A relational database stores related information in tables. A row is one complete record. A column is one kind of detail shared by all records. In a students table, name and score can be columns; one student's name and score make one row.

A primary key is a value that identifies one row, like a student number. Two students may share a name, but their IDs are different. Column types such as INTEGER, TEXT, and REAL describe the kind of value stored.

SQL is the language used to work with tables. SELECT reads rows, INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes rows, and DELETE removes rows. WHERE limits which rows are affected. Without WHERE, an update or delete can affect every row. The first example below prints SQL text; it does not run a database yet.

lesson.title: SQLite in Python: Connecting and Creating Tables
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Import Python's built-in sqlite3 library.", "Open a temporary database with sqlite3.connect(':memory:').", "Create a table and inspect its name."]
lesson.prerequisites: Level 118: Relational Databases and SQL Fundamentals
lesson.introduction: Now we will use a real database. We keep it in memory so it disappears when the program ends and leaves no practice files behind.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
sqlite3 is Python's built-in tool for SQLite databases. Import it, then call sqlite3.connect(':memory:') to open a temporary database in memory.

The connection is the open link to the database. A cursor sends SQL commands and reads their answers. You can also call connection.execute() for a short command. CREATE TABLE makes a table and lists its column names and types.

SQLite keeps a catalog named sqlite_master that describes tables. A SELECT query can ask that catalog whether your table exists. When finished, close the connection. For a database saved to disk, save changes with commit() before closing.

lesson.title: SQLite in Python: CRUD Operations
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Add rows with INSERT and read them with SELECT.", "Change or remove selected rows with UPDATE and DELETE.", "Use fetchone() for one row and fetchall() for a list of rows."]
lesson.prerequisites: Level 119: SQLite in Python: Connecting and Creating Tables
lesson.introduction: A game inventory changes as you play: you add an item, look at your items, change a count, or remove something. Those four actions are called CRUD.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
CRUD means Create, Read, Update, and Delete. INSERT adds a row. SELECT reads rows. UPDATE changes existing rows. DELETE removes rows.

A query can return one row or many rows. fetchone() gives one row as a tuple. fetchall() gives a list of all remaining rows. Use a loop to display each row in that list.

Use WHERE to choose which row to change. If you leave WHERE off UPDATE or DELETE, SQLite may change or remove every row. Use question-mark placeholders for user values; the next lesson explains why they are safer.

lesson.title: Parameterized Queries and Preventing SQL Injection
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Put ? placeholders where SQL values belong.", "Send values separately from the SQL text.", "Explain how placeholders protect user input from SQL injection."]
lesson.prerequisites: Level 120: SQLite in Python: CRUD Operations
lesson.introduction: A search box may contain ordinary words or unexpected punctuation. A placeholder tells SQLite to treat what the person typed as data, not as another SQL instruction.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
A parameterized query has a question mark where a value should go. Python sends the SQL text and values separately: execute('SELECT role FROM users WHERE username = ?', (username,)).

The comma in (username,) makes a one-item tuple. If there are two question marks, provide two values in order. SQLite puts each value into its matching place safely.

Do not join user input into SQL text. A person could type punctuation that changes the query. With placeholders, that text stays a value to search for. Table and column names usually cannot use value placeholders, so choose those from trusted options.

lesson.learning_objectives: ["Describe what Git saves in a commit.", "Recognize a commit hash as an ID for a saved change.", "Explain what a branch is used for."]
lesson.prerequisites: Level 121: Parameterized SQL Queries & Security
lesson.introduction: Imagine saving a checkpoint in a game. If a new change causes trouble, the checkpoint helps you see what changed or return to an earlier version. Git does this for project files.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
Git is a tool that records selected changes to project files. Each saved checkpoint is a commit with a message and a long unique-looking ID called a hash. A short piece of the hash is often enough to recognize a commit in a list.

A branch is a named path of work. A team can keep stable work on main and try a new feature on another branch. When the feature is ready, people can review and combine it.

Git runs as a separate command-line tool. The Python examples here store and print sample Git information; they do not run Git commands or change your repository.

lesson.title: Debugging Python Code (pdb and Breakpoints)
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Explain how a debugger helps find a mistake.", "Recognize the pdb commands n, s, c, p, and q.", "Use a breakpoint to pause a program while debugging."]
lesson.prerequisites: Level 122: Version Control with Git and GitHub
lesson.introduction: A debugger is like a pause button for a program. You can stop at a line, look at values, and move through the program one step at a time.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
Python includes pdb, a debugger that can pause a running program. Put breakpoint() on a line to pause there. At the prompt, p name shows a value, n moves to the next line, s steps into a function, c continues, and q quits.

A debugger is helpful when the final answer is wrong and you need to see where a value changed. You can inspect it at the exact line where the program is running.

The boss challenge simulates a few pdb commands because this browser editor is not an interactive terminal. It lets you practice how commands change the current line and display a value without opening a separate prompt.

lesson.title: Automated Testing with unittest
lesson.learning_objectives: ["Explain why programs use repeatable tests.", "Put checks in a unittest.TestCase class.", "Use assertions to compare an answer with what you expected."]
lesson.prerequisites: Level 123: Debugging Python Code
lesson.introduction: After fixing one bug, you want to know you did not break something else. A test is a small automatic check you can run again whenever the code changes.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
A unit test checks one small behavior, such as one function. Python's unittest library gives you a TestCase class for grouping checks. Make a class based on TestCase, then write methods whose names start with test_.

An assertion checks a result. For example, assertEqual(actual, expected) passes when the two values match. If they do not, the test runner reports a failure.

A test runner finds and runs the test methods. Running the same checks after each change is faster and more reliable than trying every feature by hand. The small challenge uses assert directly; the boss uses a unittest suite.

lesson.prerequisites: Level 124: Automated Testing with unittest
lesson.introduction: A recipe is easier to follow when its steps are neat and its ingredients are labeled. PEP 8 is a shared style guide, and type hints label the kinds of values a function expects.
lesson.detailed_explanation:
PEP 8 is Python's common style guide. It recommends four spaces for indentation, lowercase_with_underscores for functions and variables, and CapitalizedWords for classes. Consistent style makes code easier to scan.

A type hint is a note in a function definition. In def area(width: float) -> float, the hint says width is expected to be a decimal number and the result is expected to be a decimal number. The arrow points to the result type.

Python normally does not reject a value just because it disagrees with a hint. Hints help readers, editors, and separate tools find possible mistakes. They are labels, not automatic conversions or safety checks.

learning_objectives: Understand what programming is: giving step-by-step instructions to a computer
Learn your very first Python tool: the print() command
Understand WHY we need print() to see anything on screen
Learn WHAT Python does behind the scenes when reading your code
1.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed for this lesson.
1.introduction: Welcome to Python Quest! Imagine you have a friendly helper robot in your room. This robot can move at lightning speed, but it is born with a totally blank mind. It knows nothing on its own! If you say 'make tea', it freezes because it doesn't know what tea is. You must give it clear, step-by-step instructions: 1. Boil water. 2. Put tea bag in mug. 3. Pour water into mug. That is all programming is: writing down simple, numbered steps so the computer knows exactly what to do.
1.detailed_explanation:
### In simple words
A program is a list of instructions. Python follows them from top to bottom. `print()` is an instruction that shows something on the screen.

### Try it step by step
1. Write `print` in lowercase.
2. Put `(` after it and `)` at the end.
3. Put the words you want to show inside quotes: `print('Hello')`.
4. Run the program. The screen should show `Hello`.

The quotes mark the words as text. The parentheses show which value belongs to `print()`. Each new `print()` normally starts a new output line.

### More detail
🎯 WHY DO WE USE THE print() COMMAND?
Computers are silent and invisible workers. If a computer does a calculation or runs a task, it keeps the result hidden inside its memory chip. You won't see anything on your monitor! To make the computer show words or numbers on your screen, Python created a special command called `print()`. Think of `print()` as giving your computer a mouth so it can speak to you!

🤖 WHAT PYTHON DOES STEP-BY-STEP:
When Python reads: `print('System Boot')`
1. Python reads the word `print` → It realizes: 'Aha! The human wants me to display something on the screen!'
2. Python opens the parentheses `(` and looks inside.
3. Python spots the quotation marks `'...'` → It understands: 'These are human words to display, NOT code commands to execute!'
4. Python takes the exact text `System Boot` and prints it onto your screen.
5. Python automatically jumps down to a fresh line, ready for your next instruction!

⚠️ CRUCIAL RULE — CAPITALIZATION MATTERS:
Python is case-sensitive. That means lowercase `print` works, but capitalized `Print` or `PRINT` will fail with an error. Always write `print` in all-lowercase letters!

terminology.definition: Writing step-by-step instructions that tell a computer what to do.
The built-in Python tool used to display words, messages, and numbers on your screen.
The curved brackets that hold whatever message you want to display on screen.
Speech bubbles around words that tell Python 'these are words to display, not commands'.

1.syntax_breakdown:
# 1. Built-in function name: print (MUST be strictly lowercase)

learning_objectives: Understand WHY Python requires quotation marks for human words
Learn that single quotes 'hello' and double quotes "hello" work identically

2.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed for this lesson.
2.introduction: Why is Python the most popular programming language on Earth? Because it was designed to read like clean, plain English! In older languages like Java or C++, displaying a single message takes 5 to 7 complicated lines of boilerplate code. In Python, it is just one simple command! But to write Python, you need to understand how Python tells the difference between code and words.
2.detailed_explanation:
### In simple words
Python code is made of instructions, while text is information that an instruction can use. Quotes tell Python, “these are words.” Without quotes, Python treats names and symbols as instructions or values.

### Try it step by step
`print('Hello')` shows the word Hello. The quote marks do not appear in the output. Single and double quotes both work, as long as the opening and closing marks match.

Python also cares about capital letters in code: write `print`, not `Print`. The words inside quotes can use any capitalization you want.

### More detail
🎯 WHY DO WE USE QUOTATION MARKS '...' ?
Imagine you tell a robot: 'RUN'. Does that mean *run across the room*, or does it mean *say the word 'RUN' out loud*? It's confusing!
To solve this problem, programmers invented quotation marks `'...'`. Quotes act exactly like speech bubbles in a comic book:
• When Python sees quotes `'...'`, it understands: 'These are plain human words to display. Don't try to execute them as code!'
• If you forget quotes like `print(Hello)`, Python thinks Hello is a computer command name. It searches its memory, cannot find any command named Hello, and panics with an error called `NameError`!

🔍 SINGLE QUOTES VS DOUBLE QUOTES:
You can use single quotes `'Python'` or double quotes "Python". Both work 100% identically in Python! Just make sure whatever quote you start with, you close with the same quote.

⚠️ CRUCIAL RULE — CASE SENSITIVITY:
To Python, lowercase and uppercase letters are completely different symbols. `print` works, but `Print` or `PRINT` will crash. Always use lowercase!

terminology.definition: A piece of human text wrapped in quotation marks ('...' or "...").
Treating uppercase and lowercase letters as completely different symbols (print is NOT the same as Print).
An error that happens when you write a word without quotes that Python does not recognize.

3.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed for this lesson.
3.introduction: When you write code, you are not just writing for the computer—you are also writing for other humans and for future you! What if you want to leave a note in your code explaining what a line does? That is what comments are for.
3.detailed_explanation:
### In simple words
A Python file is a saved set of instructions. The Python interpreter reads the file and carries out each instruction in order. You can run a file from a code editor or from a terminal with a command such as `python my_file.py`.

### Try it step by step
1. Save Python instructions in a file ending in `.py`, such as `hello.py`.
2. Open that file in a Python editor, or open a terminal in its folder.
3. Run the file. Python starts at the first instruction and moves downward.
4. If an instruction prints text, that text appears in the output area.

A comment starts with `#`. Python skips the comment; it is a note for people reading the file. Comments do not install Python or run a program.

### More detail
🎯 WHY DO WE USE COMMENTS (#)?
What if you want to write a personal note to yourself inside your code, like 'This line prints player health'? If you write normal words in code, Python tries to run them and crashes. When you put a hash symbol `#` at the start of a line, you turn it into a **comment**. Python completely ignores it! It acts like an invisible sticky note for humans.

🤖 WHAT PYTHON DOES:
Python executes code sequentially: starting at Line 1, proceeding to Line 2, Line 3, and so forth until the end. But whenever Python spots a `#` symbol, it completely skips the rest of that line and does not print anything from it!

terminology.definition: A note written in code for humans to read. Python completely ignores comments during execution.
Processing code line by line from top to bottom in order.
A plain text file containing Python instructions that can be saved and run.

4.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed for this lesson.
4.introduction: In 1978, computer scientist Brian Kernighan wrote a tutorial that began with printing 'hello, world'. Since then, every programmer begins with this tradition! But computers were also built for calculations. Let us learn how Python handles numbers and math.
4.detailed_explanation:
### In simple words
Text and numbers can look similar but mean different things to Python. Quotes make a value into text. A number without quotes can be used in arithmetic.

### Try it step by step
`print('5 + 5')` displays the characters `5 + 5`.
`print(5 + 5)` calculates the sum and displays `10`.

Try changing one number and running the program again. Keep quotes around words such as `Hello`, but leave quotes off numbers you want Python to calculate.

### More detail
🎯 WHY DO NUMBERS HAVE NO QUOTES?
Notice this massive difference:
1. When you put numbers inside quotes: `print('5 + 5')`
   Python sees text. It displays literally: `5 + 5`
2. When you omit quotes: `print(5 + 5)`
   Python performs the calculation! It displays: `10`

Quotes tell Python: 'Treat this as plain letters to display.' Leaving off quotes tells Python: 'Calculate this mathematically!'

🤖 PYTHON'S BASIC MATH SYMBOLS:
• Addition: `+` (e.g. `10 + 5 = 15`)
• Subtraction: `-` (e.g. `20 - 4 = 16`)
• Multiplication: `*` (the asterisk symbol, e.g. `25 * 4 = 100`)
• Division: `/` (forward slash, e.g. `10 / 2 = 5.0`)

terminology.definition: A whole number without a decimal point (e.g. 5, 42, -10).
A number with a decimal point (e.g. 3.14, 0.5).
A symbol that performs an operation, like + for addition or * for multiplication.

# Numbers without quotes are evaluated mathematically by the CPU:

5.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed for this lesson.
5.introduction: So far, you have printed one piece of text at a time. But what if you want to print a word AND a calculated number together, like 'Score: 100'? In Python, you can print multiple items in a single line simply by separating them with commas!
5.detailed_explanation:
### In simple words
`print()` can show several values on one line. Separate the values with commas; Python puts a space between them by default. The `sep` setting changes that space, and `end` changes what print adds after its output.

### Try it step by step
`print('Score:', 10 + 5)` shows `Score: 15`.
`print('A', 'B', sep='-')` shows `A-B`.
`print('Loading', end='... ')` keeps the next print on the same line.

The comma separates values for `print()`. The plus sign joins or calculates values, depending on their types.

### More detail
🎯 WHY DO WE USE COMMAS INSIDE print()?
When you put commas between items inside `print()`, Python prints each item and automatically inserts a single space in between:
`print('Score:', 50 + 50)` → outputs: `Score: 100`

🔍 THE sep PARAMETER (CUSTOM SEPARATORS):
By default, Python puts a space between comma items. If you want to separate them with a hyphen or dash instead, you tell Python: `sep='-'`!
`print('Apple', 'Banana', 'Cherry', sep='-')` → outputs: `Apple-Banana-Cherry`

🔍 THE end PARAMETER (CONTROLLING LINE ENDINGS):
By default, after printing, Python presses Enter and starts the next line. If you want to stay on the same line, you pass `end='... '`!
`print('Loading', end='... ')` → stays on the same line!

terminology.definition: A value passed into a function inside parentheses, separated by commas.
A parameter in print() that specifies what symbol goes between items (default is space).
A parameter in print() that specifies what symbol goes at the end of the line (default is newline).

print('Loading', end='... ')
print('Complete!')

6.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed for this lesson.
6.introduction: In programming, any sequence of characters (letters, numbers, spaces, symbols) wrapped in quotes is called a 'string'. Think of beads strung on a necklace. You can combine and manipulate strings in powerful ways.
6.detailed_explanation:
### In simple words
A string is text inside matching quotes. The plus sign joins strings together. Python does not add a space for you, so include a space string (`' '`) when you want one.

### Try it step by step
`'Python' + 'Quest'` becomes `PythonQuest`.
`'Python' + ' ' + 'Quest'` becomes `Python Quest`.

You can also put `\n` inside a string to start a new output line. It is a special two-character code in your program that becomes a line break when printed. Keep the whole message inside one matching pair of quotes.

### More detail
🎯 WHY DO WE USE THE PLUS (+) SIGN WITH STRINGS?
When you put a plus sign `+` between two strings, Python glues them together end-to-end. This is called **concatenation**:
`print('Python' + 'Quest')` → outputs: `PythonQuest`

⚠️ CRUCIAL DIFFERENCE:
Notice that `+` does NOT insert a space automatically! If you want a space, you must add it yourself: `'Python' + ' ' + 'Quest'`.
Also: `print('5' + '5')` outputs `55`, because quotes tell Python they are text characters, not numbers!

terminology.definition: A sequence of characters enclosed in quotation marks.
The operation of joining two or more strings end-to-end using the + operator.

7.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed for this lesson.
7.introduction: Computers were originally designed as calculation engines. In Python, solving math problems is clean and instant.
7.detailed_explanation:
### In simple words
Python can calculate with numbers. Use `+` to add, `-` to subtract, `*` to multiply, and `/` to divide. Put a calculation inside `print()` to show its answer.

### Try it step by step
`print(25 * 4)` shows `100`.
Python follows normal math order: multiplication happens before addition. Use parentheses when you want to choose what happens first: `(5 + 3) * 2`.

Do not put quotes around numbers that you want Python to calculate. Quoted numbers are text.

### More detail
🎯 ORDER OF OPERATIONS IN PYTHON:
Python obeys standard order of operations: parentheses first, multiplication and division next, addition and subtraction last.
`print(10 + 5 * 2)` → evaluates `5 * 2 = 10`, then `10 + 10 = 20`!

You can print both descriptive text and calculated results together using commas:
`print('Total:', 25 * 4)` → outputs: `Total: 100`

terminology.definition: A combination of numbers, operators, and variables that Python evaluates to a single value.

8.introduction: Good code is self-explanatory, but great code includes helpful documentation for fellow engineers.
8.detailed_explanation:
### In simple words
A comment is a note for a person reading your code. Start it with `#`. Python ignores everything from that symbol to the end of the line, so a commented-out instruction will not run.

### Try it step by step
`# show the score` is only a note.
`print(15 * 6)` is an instruction and displays `90`.
To temporarily stop a line from running, put `#` at the beginning of that line. Remove the `#` when you want it to run again.

### More detail
🎯 WHY DO WE USE COMMENTS?
Comments allow you to:
1. Explain what complex code is doing in simple human words.
2. Provide section headers so your file is organized.
3. Temporarily 'comment out' code during testing to prevent bugs without deleting it.

9.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed for this lesson.
9.introduction: Every human language has grammar rules: spelling, punctuation, and capitalization. In programming, these rules are called syntax.
9.detailed_explanation:
### In simple words
Python expects code to follow exact spelling and punctuation rules. A missing quote or parenthesis can stop the program before it runs. Capitalization matters for Python names such as `print`.

### Try it step by step
Before running a line, check that every opening quote has a matching closing quote, every `(` has a `)`, and names such as `print` use the correct lowercase letters.

At the start of a program, write each top-level line from the left edge. Spaces at the start are used for grouping code inside blocks, which you will learn later.

### More detail
🎯 THE 3 MOST COMMON BEGINNER ERRORS AND HOW TO AVOID THEM:
1. Unclosed quotes: `print('Hello)` → You opened `'` but forgot to close it with another `'` before the bracket!
2. Unclosed parenthesis: `print('Hello'` → You opened `(` but forgot to close it with `)` at the end!
3. Accidental leading spaces: In Python, you must not add random spaces at the very start of a line, or Python will raise an `IndentationError`!

11.title: What Are Variables?
11.learning_objectives: ["Understand how computers store information in memory (RAM)", "Learn what a variable is and why programmers use them", "Understand variables as labeled containers or name tags referencing data", "Distinguish between a variable name and its stored value"]
11.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed.
11.introduction: A variable is a name that points to a value. Think of it like a labeled box: the label helps you find what you stored. In `hero_title = 'Python Explorer'`, the name is hero_title, the equals sign stores the value, and the value is text. You can use the name later instead of typing the value again.
11.detailed_explanation:
hero_title = 'Python Explorer'
print(hero_title)

The first line stores text under the name hero_title. The second line asks Python to show that value. The screen says Python Explorer. Quotes mark text values; when you want the value from a variable, write its name without quotes.

Another example:
coins = 25
print(coins)

This stores the number 25 and displays it. A variable can hold text, numbers, and other kinds of values.

12.title: Creating Variables
12.learning_objectives: ["Master creating variables with descriptive, readable names", "Understand how Python allocates memory automatically", "Understand multiple assignments in a single statement"]
12.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed.
12.introduction: In Python, create a variable with a name, an equals sign, and a value. Python works out the kind of value for you. You can assign two related variables on one line: `start_x, start_y = 0, 10` stores 0 in start_x and 10 in start_y, in that order.
12.detailed_explanation:
start_x, start_y = 0, 10
print(f'Position: {start_x}, {start_y}')

Python matches values from left to right: 0 goes into start_x and 10 goes into start_y. The f-string displays both values with a comma between them. You may also put each assignment on its own line. One-line assignment is handy when related values are created together.

13.title: Variable Naming Rules
13.learning_objectives: ["Learn Python's strict rules for legal variable names", "Understand why variable names cannot start with a digit", "Master snake_case naming conventions (PEP 8)", "Identify Python reserved keywords that cannot be used as names"]
13.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed.
13.introduction: A variable name can use letters, numbers, and underscores, but cannot begin with a number. Names cannot contain spaces, and Python special words cannot be used as names. Uppercase and lowercase are different, so score and Score are separate names. Use underscores between words, like favorite_language.
13.detailed_explanation:
favorite_language = 'Python'
first_score = 90
player_name = 'Alex'

These are valid names. Names like 2score, player name, and first-score are invalid because they start with a number or contain a space or hyphen. Python reports a syntax error when it cannot read a name. Choose a clear name and spell it the same way each time.

14.title: Updating Variables
14.learning_objectives: ["Understand that variables can be updated and reassigned over time", "Learn how Python evaluates the right side of = before updating the left", "Master augmented assignment operators (+=, -=, *=, /=)"]
14.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed.
14.introduction: A variable can be updated after it is created. The short form `coins += 25` means add 25 to the current value and save the answer back in coins. This is useful for scores, health, and counters that change while a program runs.
14.detailed_explanation:
coins = 50
coins += 25
print(coins)

After line one, coins is 50. The next line adds 25 and saves 75 back in coins. The last line displays 75. `coins -= 10` subtracts 10; `coins *= 2` multiplies by 2. The equals sign means the updated answer is stored in the variable.

15.title: Understanding Integers
15.learning_objectives: ["Understand the int data type in Python", "Learn that Python integers have arbitrary precision (no overflow)", "Use underscores as visual digit separators in large numbers (e.g. 1_000_000)"]
15.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed.
15.introduction: An integer is a whole number with no decimal part, such as 0, 7, or -12. Python calls it an int. Integers are useful for counts, ages, and scores. Underscores can make large numbers easier to read: `1_000_000` has the same value as `1000000`.
15.detailed_explanation:
credits = 1_000_000
print(credits)

The underscores help a person read the number; Python ignores them. The output is 1000000. You can do arithmetic with integers too: `total = 12 + 8` stores 20. Use a float when the number needs a decimal part.

17.title: Formatting Strings with f-strings
17.learning_objectives: ["Store text in variables using str data type", "Learn string length using the len() function", "Format variables into strings using f-strings"]
17.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed.
17.introduction: A string is text between matching quote marks. An f-string mixes text and variable values: put f before the quote, then put a variable inside curly braces where its value should appear.
17.detailed_explanation:
player = 'Mia'
gold = 12
print(f'Player {player} has {gold} gold')

Python replaces {player} with Mia and {gold} with 12, so the output is Player Mia has 12 gold. The braces are instructions and do not appear in the output. Without f, Python would show the braces as text. `len(text)` counts the characters in a string.

20.prerequisites: No prior Python knowledge is needed.
20.introduction: Sometimes a number arrives as text, such as from a form. Python cannot do arithmetic with the text '100' until you convert it. `int(text)` makes a whole number and `float(text)` makes a decimal number. The text must contain a suitable number.

22.introduction: A program can ask you for information while it runs. Python's `input()` pauses and waits for a person to type a line and press Enter. The text inside `input('Your name: ')` is a prompt: it tells the person what to type. The answer is saved in a variable so the program can use it.

`input()` always gives back text, even if the person types digits. This level uses text answers. The next level shows how to turn digit text into a number for math.

24.title: Understanding int() and float()
learning_objectives: Explain why input() returns text
Use int() to convert whole-number text

24.introduction: An answer from `input()` is text. If someone types 20, Python receives the text '20', not the number 20. To calculate with it, wrap input() in `int()` for a whole number or `float()` for a number that may have a decimal part.
24.detailed_explanation:
Example with a whole number:
age = int(input())
print(f'Next year you will be {age + 1}')

If the person types 19, input() first reads the text '19'. int() changes it to the number 19. Python can add 1, so it prints Next year you will be 20.

Example with a decimal:
price = float(input())
print(price)

If the person types 2.50, float() makes it a decimal number. Use int() for counts and ages; use float() for prices or measurements that can include a decimal. The typed answer must look like a number or Python reports an error.

25.title: Arithmetic Operators
learning_objectives: Recognize the arithmetic symbols
Use // to find the whole-number quotient

25.introduction: Python can do arithmetic with numbers. The main symbols are `+` add, `-` subtract, `*` multiply, `/` divide, `//` divide into whole groups, `%` find what is left over, and `**` raise a number to a power. Use the symbol that matches the calculation you need.
25.detailed_explanation:
Complete example:
a = 17
b = 5
print(a + b)
print(a // b)
print(a % b)

The answers are 22, 3, and 2. `17 // 5` asks how many full groups of 5 fit in 17. Three groups fit. `17 % 5` asks what remains, which is 2.

More examples: `6 * 4` gives 24, `8 / 2` gives 4.0, and `2 ** 3` gives 8. Division with / can produce a decimal. Floor division // gives the whole-number quotient.

26.title: Assignment Operators
learning_objectives: Use +=, -=, and *= to update a variable

26.introduction: An assignment operator updates a variable and saves the new value. For example, `score += 5` means add 5 to score and keep the answer in score. This is a shorter way to write `score = score + 5`. Python has similar shortcuts for subtracting, multiplying, and dividing.
26.detailed_explanation:
Complete example:
score = 10
score += 5
score *= 2
print(score)

First score is 10. `score += 5` changes it to 15. `score *= 2` changes the current 15 to 30. The output is 30. Each shortcut uses the current value, does the calculation, and stores the answer back in the same variable.

Other shortcuts include `-=`, `/=`, `//=`, `%=`, and `**=`. The order matters because every step updates the value used by the next step.

27.title: Comparison Operators
learning_objectives: Use comparison symbols to ask questions about values
Tell == apart from =
Understand that comparisons give True or False
27.introduction: A comparison checks how two values relate and gives the answer `True` or `False`. Use `==` to check if values are equal, `!=` for not equal, and `<`, `>`, `<=`, or `>=` to compare size. A single `=` stores a value; two equals signs `==` ask a question.
27.detailed_explanation:
Complete example:
score = 75
print(score >= 50)
print(score == 100)

The first comparison asks whether 75 is at least 50, so Python prints True. The second asks whether 75 equals 100, so it prints False.

You can chain comparisons to check a range: `10 <= number <= 50` means number is at least 10 and at most 50. The endpoints are included. A comparison does not change the values; it gives a True or False answer.

Checks whether two values are the same.

28.title: Logical Operators
learning_objectives: Use and when both conditions must be true

28.introduction: Sometimes a program makes a decision using more than one yes-or-no answer. `and` means both checks must be True. `or` means at least one check must be True. `not` flips an answer: True becomes False, and False becomes True.
28.detailed_explanation:
Complete example:
age = 20
has_ticket = True
allowed = age >= 18 and has_ticket
print(allowed)

The person is at least 18, so the first check is True. They also have a ticket, so the second check is True. With `and`, both must be True; allowed becomes True.

For `or`, one True answer is enough: `has_ticket or is_vip`. For `not`, `not is_banned` is True when is_banned is False. Use parentheses to make a longer decision easier to read.

29.title: Operator Precedence
learning_objectives: Explain why Python follows a calculation order
Use parentheses to choose what happens first
Work through a mixed calculation step by step
29.introduction: When a calculation has several operations, Python follows a set order so it gets the same answer every time. Parentheses are done first, then powers, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. Use parentheses when you want to make the order especially clear.
29.detailed_explanation:
Compare these calculations:
print(2 + 3 * 4)
print((2 + 3) * 4)

The first answer is 14 because Python multiplies 3 by 4 before adding 2. The second answer is 20 because the parentheses tell Python to add 2 and 3 first.

A useful order to remember is: parentheses, powers (**), multiplication or division (*, /, //, %), then addition or subtraction (+, -). If two operations have the same priority, Python usually works from left to right. Parentheses can make your intention easier to see.

40.title: What Are Loops?
40.learning_objectives: ["Understand what loops and iteration are in computer programming", "Understand the DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principle", "Recognize the two primary loop types in Python: while and for"]
40.introduction: Imagine being asked to write 'I will write clean Python code' 1,000 times by hand. It would take hours of tedious, mind-numbing effort. But for a computer, repeating a task 1,000 times takes less than a millisecond! Loops are the engine of repetition in programming.
40.detailed_explanation:
What Are Loops?

1. `🔄 The Conveyor Belt Analogy`: Imagine stamping 1,000 envelopes by hand. A loop is a machine that stamps each envelope automatically until the stack is done!
2. `⚡ Massive Efficiency`: With 2 lines of loop code, you can print 1,000 lines or process 1,000,000 numbers in seconds.
3. `🔁 2 Types in Python`: `for` loops (count through items) and `while` loops (repeat until a condition changes).

41.title: Understanding while Loops
41.learning_objectives: ["Master the syntax of the while loop in Python", "Understand loop variables, initialization, and loop incrementers", "Learn how to guarantee loop termination"]
41.introduction: A `while` loop is like an `if` statement that refuses to leave! When an `if` statement is True, it runs once and finishes. When a `while` loop is True, it runs, goes back to the top, checks the condition again, and repeats as long as the condition stays True.
41.detailed_explanation:
How `while` Loops Work:

1. `⏱️ Keep Going While True`: Think of musical chairs: as long as the music plays (`while music_playing:`), keep running around chairs!
2. `⚠️ The Counter is Essential`: You MUST change something inside the loop (`countdown -= 1`) so the condition eventually turns False!
3. `🛑 Stop Test`: As soon as `countdown` hits 0, `countdown > 0` becomes False and Python jumps past the loop.

Once it becomes False, the loop stops."}, {"term": "Counter Variable", "definition": "⏱️ Lap Counter: A number (like count += 1) updated on each round so the loop knows when to stop."}]

42.title: Understanding for Loops
42.learning_objectives: ["Master the syntax of for loops in Python", "Understand how Python iterates directly over items without manual counters", "Iterate over characters in a string"]
42.introduction: In many languages, running a loop requires declaring counters, conditions, and incrementers manually. In Python, `for` loops are fundamentally different: they iterate directly over sequences of items! It reads like plain English: 'For each item in this collection, do this.'
42.detailed_explanation:
How `for` Loops Work:

1. `🎒 The Backpack Analogy`: You have a backpack with 3 fruits. The `for` loop takes out `'Apple'`, runs your code, takes out `'Banana'`, runs your code, and finishes when the bag is empty!
2. `🚫 No Counter Needed`: Unlike `while`, a `for` loop never gets stuck in an infinite loop—it automatically stops when all items are visited.
3. `🧵 Strings are Iterables too!`: Looping over `'CAT'` prints `'C'`, then `'A'`, then `'T'` on separate lines!

43.title: Understanding range()
43.learning_objectives: ["Master the range() built-in generator function", "Understand 1-argument range(stop), 2-argument range(start, stop), and 3-argument range(start, stop, step)", "Learn why the stop parameter is exclusive (up to, but not including stop)", "Generate descending reverse sequences using negative steps"]
43.introduction: What if you want a `for` loop to run 100 times, or count from 10 to 50, or count by 5s? You don't want to type out a list of 100 numbers by hand! In Python, the `range()` function generates arithmetic numeric sequences on demand with incredible memory efficiency.
43.detailed_explanation:
Mastering the `range()` Generator:

1. `🚫 Stop Number is Excluded`: In Python, `range(1, 5)` stops BEFORE 5! It produces `1, 2, 3, 4`.
2. `🦘 The Step Parameter`: The third number controls the jump size: `range(10, 0, -1)` counts BACKWARDS from 10 down to 1!
3. `⚡ Ultra Fast`: `range()` doesn't create 1,000,000 numbers in memory at once—it generates each number on the fly as the loop spins.

44.title: break Statement
44.learning_objectives: ["Understand how the break keyword works in both for and while loops", "Prematurely terminate a loop when a target item or error condition is encountered", "Recognize that execution jumps immediately to the line following the loop block"]
44.introduction: Imagine searching through a deck of 52 playing cards for the Ace of Spades. Once you find it on card #7, do you keep searching through the remaining 45 cards? Of course not! You stop searching immediately. In Python, `break` lets you bail out of a loop the instant you have found what you need.
44.detailed_explanation:
The `break` Statement:

1. `🚨 The Emergency Brake`: When Python sees `break`, it stops the loop dead in its tracks right now!
2. `🔍 Search Optimization`: If you are searching a database of 1,000,000 items and find the user at item #5, use `break` so you don't waste time checking the other 999,995 items.
3. `🛑 Exits Only the Current Loop`: In nested loops, `break` only exits the innermost loop it is placed in.

45.title: continue Statement
45.learning_objectives: ["Understand how the continue statement differs from break", "Skip unwanted or invalid items without terminating the entire loop", "Filter sequences during iteration cleanly"]
45.introduction: While `break` says 'I am quitting this entire loop right now!', `continue` says 'I am skipping ONLY this specific item—let's move on to the next one!'
45.detailed_explanation:
The `continue` Statement:

1. `⏭️ The Skip Button`: Unlike `break` which destroys the loop, `continue` just skips whatever code is below it in the CURRENT round and starts the next round.
2. `🧹 Bypassing Bad Data`: If an item in your list is `None` or corrupt, call `continue` to skip it safely without crashing your program.
3. `💡 Code Simplifier`: Reduces deep indentation by getting invalid cases out of the way early.

46.title: Nested Loops

46.introduction: How does a digital clock display time? For every 1 hour that passes, the minute hand ticks through 60 minutes! And for every 1 minute, the second hand ticks 60 seconds! That is a nested loop: an inner loop cycling fully for every single tick of an outer loop.
46.detailed_explanation:
Nested Loops:

1. `🎡 The Clock Analogy`: Think of hours and minutes. For every 1 hour (outer loop), the minute hand (inner loop) must tick through all 60 minutes!
2. `🗺️ 2D Grids & Games`: Nested loops are how video games draw checkerboards, tile maps, and matrices.
3. `⚡ Be Mindful of Scale`: If outer loop runs 100 times and inner runs 100 times, the code inside runs 10,000 times!

47.title: Infinite Loops and Prevention
47.learning_objectives: ["Understand what causes an infinite loop in computer software", "Identify non-terminating while loop conditions", "Use timeout guards, maximum iteration caps, and break conditions to prevent infinite loops"]
47.introduction: Have you ever seen an app freeze, showing a spinning beach ball or 'Not Responding' dialog? In many cases, that freeze is caused by an infinite loop: a loop that never reaches a stopping condition and runs forever, eating 100% of a CPU core.
47.detailed_explanation:
Preventing Infinite Loops:

1. `🌀 The Runaway Train Bug`: Writing `while count < 5:` but forgetting to type `count += 1` means count stays 0 forever! The loop will freeze your screen.
2. `🛡️ Circuit Breakers`: In production code, always have a maximum safety counter to prevent infinite loops.
3. `⌨️ How to Stop`: If a runaway script occurs in terminal, press `Ctrl + C` to kill execution immediately.
47.terminology: [{"term": "Infinite Loop", "definition": "🌀 Runaway Train: A loop whose condition never becomes False, running forever until the computer runs out of memory or you kill it."}, {"term": "Circuit Breaker", "definition": "🛡️ Safety Fuse: A safety counter that automatically breaks out of a while loop after a safe maximum number of laps (e.g. 100)."}]
47.syntax_breakdown:
# Safe while loop with circuit breaker:
count = 0
safety_fuse = 0
while count < 5:
    print('Running step:', count)
    count += 1
    safety_fuse += 1
    if safety_fuse > 50:
        print('Safety trip activated!')
        break

49.title: String Slicing and Indexing
learning_objectives: Read one character using a positive or negative index.
Take a substring with a slice and explain its included start and excluded stop.
Use omitted bounds, steps, and reverse slicing.
Distinguish IndexError from a slice clipped at the end.
49.prerequisites: Know that quotes make a string and a variable can store it. Level 49 builds on variables; Level 50 will clean strings.
49.introduction: A game receives the code word PYTHON and needs its first and last letters. Direct indexing gets one character; a slice gets a piece such as YTH. Python assigns each character a position so you can ask for exactly what you need.
49.detailed_explanation:
A character is one letter, digit, space, or symbol in text. Its index is its position. Python starts indexes at 0: the first character is text[0], the second is text[1]. Negative indexes count backward, with -1 meaning the last character and -2 the one before it.

Use text[index] for exactly one character. If that position does not exist, Python raises IndexError. For example, 'cat'[8] fails. A slice uses text[start:stop]. The start is included and stop is excluded: 'PYTHON'[1:4] includes positions 1, 2, and 3, giving YTH.

Leave start empty to begin at the first character; leave stop empty to continue to the end. Slices that extend past the text are clipped to the available characters, unlike a direct index. A third part is the step: text[start:stop:step]. Step 2 takes every second character; step -1 walks backward, so text[::-1] reverses the string. Slicing returns new text and leaves the original unchanged.

terminology.definition: One letter, digit, space, or symbol in text.
The zero-based position of one character; -1 is the last.
A selected range written with start, stop, and optionally step.
An error from asking for one character at a position that does not exist.

49.syntax_breakdown:
text[index]             # one character
text[start:stop]        # start included, stop excluded
text[start:stop:step]
text[:3]                # from the start, before index 3
text[3:]                # from index 3 through the end
text[::2]               # every second character
text[::-1]              # reverse the text

practical_examples.title: Get the first and last character
practical_examples.code:
text = 'PYTHON'
print(text[0])
print(text[-1])
practical_examples.explanation: Index 0 is the first character. Index -1 is always the last, even if the word length changes.

practical_examples.title: Slice, skip, and reverse
practical_examples.code:
text = 'PYTHON'
print(text[1:4])
print(text[:2])
print(text[4:])
print(text[::2])
print(text[::-1])
practical_examples.explanation: The slice stops before its stop index. The step chooses every second character; -1 walks backward.

practical_examples.title: A long slice is clipped safely
practical_examples.code:
text = 'cat'
print(text[1:99])
practical_examples.explanation: The slice ends at the text's actual end. By contrast, text[99] raises IndexError.

line_by_line.explanation: Store the six-character string in text.
Read index 0, the first character, and display it.
Read index -1, the last character, and display it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using text[1] for the first character.
common_mistakes.why: Index 1 means the second character because counting starts at 0.
common_mistakes.fix: Use text[0].

common_mistakes.mistake: Expecting the stop index in text[1:4] to appear.
common_mistakes.why: The start is included but the stop is excluded.
common_mistakes.fix: Use text[1:5] to include positions 1 through 4.

common_mistakes.mistake: Expecting text[99:100] to raise IndexError.
common_mistakes.why: A slice clips to the available range; direct indexing requires an existing position.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a slice for a range, and check length before a possibly invalid direct index.

49.real_world_apps: Inspect a product code's first character, take an extension from the end of a filename, or extract a known section from a longer code. Use an index for one character and a slice for a range.
49.summary: Indexes select one character: positive indexes start at 0 and negative indexes start at -1 from the end. Slices include start and exclude stop; they can use a step. Direct indexing can raise IndexError, while an overlong slice is clipped.

50.title: Essential String Methods
learning_objectives: Call strip(), lower(), upper(), and replace() with method syntax.
Explain that string methods return new strings because strings are immutable.
Save a returned string and chain methods in a useful order.
Use methods to clean typed names or create a simple URL slug.
50.prerequisites: Know variables, strings, and print(). Level 49 taught how to select parts of text; this lesson returns cleaned versions of text.
50.introduction: People can type a name with extra spaces or different capital letters. A program may need one consistent version before comparing or displaying it. String methods are built-in actions for cleaning and changing text.
50.detailed_explanation:
A method is an action called on a value. The dot connects the string to the method, and parentheses call it: name.lower(). strip() removes whitespace from the two ends, not between words. lower() and upper() return text with letters changed to one case. replace(old, new) returns text with matching pieces replaced.

Strings are immutable: a method does not edit the original string in place. It returns a new string. If name is 'SAM', name.lower() produces 'sam', but name remains 'SAM' unless you save the result. Write cleaned = name.strip().lower() when you want to keep the cleaned value.

Chaining runs methods left to right: name.strip().lower() first removes edge whitespace, then lowercases the returned string. Order matters. For a web slug, lowercase the title and replace spaces with hyphens. Use a method when its returned result is useful; otherwise it is easy to call it and accidentally discard the result.

terminology.definition: An action called on a value with dot syntax, such as text.lower().
The new value a method gives back.
Not changeable in place; string methods return new strings.
Calling a method on the result of another method.
Spaces, tabs, or line breaks; strip() removes it from the ends.

50.syntax_breakdown:
text.strip()                 # remove whitespace at the ends
text.lower()                 # return lowercase text
text.upper()                 # return uppercase text
text.replace(old, new)       # replace matching text
clean = text.strip().lower() # save the chained result

print(clean_name)
practical_examples.explanation: strip() removes outside spaces, then lower() changes the letters. The final new string is saved in clean_name; raw_name is unchanged.

practical_examples.title: Create a simple slug
practical_examples.code:

slug = title.lower().replace(' ', '-')
print(slug)
practical_examples.explanation: lower() returns lowercase text; replace() changes each space to a hyphen.

practical_examples.title: See that the original stays the same
practical_examples.code:

new_word = word.lower()
print(word)
print(new_word)
practical_examples.explanation: lower() returns another string. The old variable still refers to 'Cat'.

line_by_line.explanation: Store the typed name, including its outside spaces.
Remove edge spaces, lowercase the returned text, and save the final result.
Display the cleaned string sam.

common_mistakes.why: That refers to the method instead of calling it.
common_mistakes.fix: Write name.lower().

common_mistakes.mistake: Calling name.lower() and expecting name to change.
common_mistakes.why: Strings are immutable; lower() returns a new string.
common_mistakes.fix: Save the result: name = name.lower().

common_mistakes.why: strip() removes whitespace only at the two ends.
common_mistakes.fix: Use replace() or split() and join() for spaces inside text.

common_mistakes.fix: Use title.replace(' ', '-').

50.real_world_apps: Trim accidental spaces from a username before checking it. Compare lowercase names so capitalization does not create accidental differences. Turn a page title into a simple URL slug by replacing spaces with hyphens.
50.summary: String methods use dot-and-parentheses syntax. strip(), lower(), upper(), and replace() return new strings rather than changing the original. Save returned text; chaining runs from left to right.

51.title: Format Text and Numbers
learning_objectives: Insert variables and calculations into text with an f-string.
Use .2f to display two decimal places without changing the stored number.
Align text and numbers with a field width.
Print literal braces by doubling them.
51.prerequisites: Know variables, strings, numbers, and basic arithmetic. Level 50 covered string methods; an f-string assembles output from current values.
51.introduction: A receipt needs to show an item name and price. Joining text by hand is awkward when values change or need fixed decimal places. An f-string lets Python place values into a sentence and format them for display.
51.detailed_explanation:
An f-string begins with f immediately before its quote. Inside braces, Python evaluates an expression and inserts its value. For example, {name} looks up the current value of name; {quantity * price} calculates a total. Without the f prefix, braces are ordinary text.

A colon inside braces starts a format specification. .2f means show a fixed-point number with two digits after the decimal, so 4.5 is displayed as 4.50. This changes the displayed text, not the number stored in the variable.

A width reserves a minimum number of character spaces. In {item:<8}, < means left-align and 8 is the minimum field width. In {price:>7.2f}, > means right-align, 7 is the minimum width, and .2f controls decimals. Long text is not cut off; it may extend beyond its field. For literal braces, double them: f'{{ready}}' displays {ready}.

Use f-strings to build messages, receipts, and reports. Keep the value as a number while calculating; format it when displaying it.

terminology.definition: A string prefixed by f that evaluates expressions inside braces.
Code that Python evaluates to produce a value, such as quantity * price.
Instructions after a colon that control how a value is displayed.
The number of digits shown after a decimal point for fixed-point formatting.
A minimum display width and where the value sits: < left, > right, ^ center.

51.syntax_breakdown:
name = 'Mia'
price = 4.5
print(f'{name} pays ${price:.2f}')
# {name} inserts the variable's value.
# :.2f displays two digits after the decimal.
# {item:<8} left-aligns in a minimum width of 8.
# {price:>7.2f} right-aligns in a minimum width of 7.

practical_examples.title: Insert variables into a message
practical_examples.code:

practical_examples.explanation: The f prefix tells Python to evaluate each expression in braces, then insert the result into the sentence.

practical_examples.title: Display a price to two decimal places
practical_examples.code:

print(f'Price: ${price:.2f}')
practical_examples.explanation: .2f displays two digits after the decimal. The value in price remains the number 4.5.

practical_examples.title: Align a name and a price
practical_examples.code:
item = 'Tea'
price = 2.5
print(f'{item:<8}|${price:>6.2f}')
practical_examples.explanation: The item is left-aligned in 8 spaces. The price is right-aligned in a minimum width of 6 and displayed with two decimals.

practical_examples.title: Calculate inside braces
practical_examples.code:

price = 2.5
print(f'Total: ${quantity * price:.2f}')
practical_examples.explanation: Python multiplies the values inside the braces, then formats the result.

Store the score as a number.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the f before the quote.
common_mistakes.why: Without f, braces are ordinary text and variables are not inserted.
common_mistakes.fix: Write print(f'Hello, {name}').

common_mistakes.mistake: Putting a variable name in quotes inside its braces.
common_mistakes.why: That asks Python to insert the literal word rather than look up the variable.
common_mistakes.fix: Use {name}, not {'name'}, when name is a variable.

common_mistakes.mistake: Thinking .2f changes the stored number.
common_mistakes.why: The format spec changes only the text shown by the f-string.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a width truncates long text.
common_mistakes.why: Width is a minimum; longer values extend beyond it.
common_mistakes.fix: Choose enough width for typical values and handle unusually long labels separately.

51.real_world_apps: Receipts align product names and prices. Score reports insert a student's name and show an average with a consistent number of decimal places. Tables become easier to scan when columns line up.
51.summary: Prefix text with f and put values or calculations in braces. A colon introduces display rules: .2f chooses two decimals, while < and > align within a minimum-width field. Formatting affects display, not the stored value.

52.title: Introduction to Lists
learning_objectives: Create an ordered list and identify its items.
Read an item by its zero-based index and count items with len().
Use a for loop to visit items one by one.
Change a list item and explain that lists are mutable.
Create and use an empty list.
52.prerequisites: Know variables, strings, numbers, and how a for loop repeats. Lists let one variable hold an ordered group of values.
52.introduction: A game inventory may contain a map, a potion, and a key. Separate variables become awkward as the inventory grows. A list stores related items together, remembers their order, and lets a program visit or change them.
52.detailed_explanation:
A list is an ordered, mutable collection. Write items between square brackets and separate them with commas: items = ['map', 'potion']. Each stored value is an item or element. Order matters because each item has a position.

Use square brackets with an index to read one item. Indexes start at zero, so items[0] is the first item. Negative indexes count backward: items[-1] is the last. len(items) returns the number of items. An empty list is [] and has length 0.

A for loop visits every item in order: for item in items: gives the current item to item on each pass. This works even if the list later grows or shrinks, unlike manually writing several print statements.

Lists are mutable: you can replace an item with items[0] = 'torch'. Lists can also grow and shrink with methods, which Level 53 teaches. Use a list when order matters, repeated values are allowed, or the group will change. A set or dictionary fits different needs.

terminology.definition: An ordered collection written with square brackets.
One value stored in a collection.
A zero-based position used to read or replace one item.
The item count returned by len(list_name).
Able to change after creation.
Visiting items one at a time, often with a for loop.

52.syntax_breakdown:
items = ['map', 'potion'] # create a list
items[0]                 # read the first item
items[0] = 'torch'       # replace an item
len(items)               # count items
for item in items:       # visit items in order
    print(item)
empty = []               # create an empty list

Read index 0, the first item, and display apple.

53.title: List Operations and Methods
learning_objectives: Replace a list item by index.
Add one item with append(), several with extend(), or one at a position with insert().
Remove by position with pop() or by value with remove().
Sort in place and explain which methods return a value versus None.
53.prerequisites: Know list indexes, loops, and mutability. This lesson explains methods for changing a list; Level 54 covers slices and copies.
53.introduction: A game inventory changes as a player finds, uses, or reorganizes items. List methods are ready-made actions for those changes. The right method depends on whether you have one new item, several items, a position, or a value to remove.
53.detailed_explanation:
Call a list method with a dot: bag.append('key'). append() adds its argument as one item at the end. extend() visits another collection and adds each of its items. insert(index, item) places one item before the given position. Item assignment, such as bag[0] = 'map', replaces one existing position rather than adding a new one.

pop() removes and returns an item. With no index it removes the last item; pop(0) removes the first. Save the return value if it is needed. remove(value) searches for the first matching value and removes it; if the value is absent, Python raises ValueError.

sort() rearranges the same list in ascending order and returns None. append(), extend(), insert(), remove(), and sort() also change the list and return None. Do not write bag = bag.sort(): that assigns None to bag. Call bag.sort() on its own. sorted(bag) is different: it returns a new sorted list and leaves bag unchanged.

Choose a method based on the job: append one value, extend from several values, insert at a position, pop by position, remove by value, or sort the current list. Check indexes and values before trying to remove them.

terminology.definition: A method changes the existing list rather than returning a replacement list.
Adds its argument as one item at the end.
Adds each item from another iterable.
Removes and returns an item; with no index, removes the last.
Removes the first matching value.
Python's value meaning no result; in-place list methods return None.

53.syntax_breakdown:

items.append(value)          # add one at end
items.extend(more_items)     # add each item
items.insert(index, value)  # insert before index
removed = items.pop()       # remove and return last
items.remove(value)         # remove first matching value
items.sort()                # reorder this list in place
new_order = sorted(items)   # make a separate sorted list
