54.title: List Slicing and Copying
learning_objectives: Slice a list with included start and excluded stop positions.
Predict what happens when two names refer to the same list.
Make a shallow copy with copy() or [:].
Explain the shallow-copy limit when a list contains mutable inner lists.
54.prerequisites: Know list indexing and methods. String slices from Level 49 use the same bounds; this lesson applies slicing to lists and explains copying.
54.introduction: A program may need a few middle entries from a list, or a safe working version to edit without changing the saved one. Slicing selects a range. Copying separates the outer list. These tools help avoid surprising changes to shared data.
54.detailed_explanation:
A slice uses list[start:stop:step]. The start is included and stop is excluded. items[1:-1] therefore leaves off the first and last values. Leaving out a bound starts at the beginning or continues to the end. A slice creates a new outer list containing the selected items.

Assignment does not copy a list. After second = first, both names refer to the same list. This is aliasing. An append or item assignment through either name is visible through both names.

Use first.copy() or first[:] to make a shallow copy. The outer list is new, so adding or replacing a top-level item in the copy does not change the original outer list. A shallow copy does not copy nested mutable objects. If an item is another list, both outer lists still refer to that same inner list. Changing that inner list is visible through both. Deep copying is a separate tool and is outside this lesson.

Use a slice to select a portion; use a shallow copy for a separate outer list; use simple assignment when shared changes are intended. Always consider whether the items themselves contain mutable objects.

terminology.definition: A selected range; start is included and stop is excluded.
The connection from a variable name to the object it refers to.
Two or more names refer to the same object.
A new outer list whose nested objects are still shared.
Changing an existing object's contents.

54.syntax_breakdown:
items[start:stop:step]
items[1:-1]        # omit first and last
second = first     # both names refer to the same list
second = first.copy() # shallow copy
second = first[:]     # another shallow-copy form
# Inner lists are still shared by a shallow copy.

practical_examples.title: Take the middle items
practical_examples.code:
colors = ['red', 'blue', 'green', 'gold']
inside = colors[1:-1]
print(inside)
print(colors)
practical_examples.explanation: The slice begins at index 1 and stops before index -1. It returns a new list with blue and green; colors is unchanged.

practical_examples.title: Assignment shares; copy() separates the outer list
practical_examples.code:
original = ['red', 'blue']
alias = original
copy = original.copy()
alias.append('gold')
copy.append('green')
print(original)
print(copy)
practical_examples.explanation: alias shares original, so gold appears in original. copy is a separate outer list, so adding green to it does not change original.

practical_examples.title: A shallow copy shares inner lists
practical_examples.code:
original = [[1], [2]]
copy = original.copy()
copy[0].append(9)
print(original)
print(copy)
practical_examples.explanation: The two outer lists are separate, but their first item refers to the same inner list. Appending 9 through copy is visible through original too.

line_by_line.explanation: Create a list with four ordered color names.
Take a new list beginning at index 1 and stopping before the last item.
Display the two selected middle items.
Display the original to show slicing did not remove any of its items.

common_mistakes.mistake: Thinking second = first copies a list.
common_mistakes.why: Assignment creates another name for the same object.
common_mistakes.fix: Use first.copy() or first[:] for a shallow copy.

common_mistakes.mistake: Expecting items[1:3] to include index 3.
common_mistakes.why: The stop index is excluded.
common_mistakes.fix: Use items[1:4] to include positions 1, 2, and 3.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming copy() duplicates every nested list.
common_mistakes.why: copy() makes a shallow copy and keeps references to inner objects.
common_mistakes.fix: Remember that changing a shared inner list affects both outer lists.

54.real_world_apps: A history screen can display only recent actions with a slice. A program can make a copy of a shopping list before proposing edits. Nested records require extra care because a shallow copy still shares inner lists or dictionaries.
54.summary: Slices select ranges with an included start and excluded stop. Assignment shares a list. copy() and [:] create shallow copies: the outer list is new, but nested mutable items remain shared.
practice_questions: If b = a and b.append(4), does a change? Check: yes; they refer to the same list.
Does a.copy() recursively copy nested lists? Check: no, it is shallow.
Which creates a separate outer list, a[:] or b = a? Check: a[:].

55.title: Introduction to Tuples
learning_objectives: Create a tuple and read values by index.
Explain that a tuple is ordered but its positions cannot be reassigned.
Create a one-item tuple using a trailing comma.
Choose a tuple for a fixed group and a list for a group that changes.
Recognize that a mutable object inside a tuple can still change.
55.prerequisites: Know variables, lists, and indexes. A tuple resembles a list but is chosen when its positions should stay fixed.
55.introduction: A map coordinate has an x and y value that belong together. If the pair should keep its order and not have one position replaced accidentally, a tuple is a suitable container.
55.detailed_explanation:
A tuple is an ordered collection, often written with parentheses and commas: point = (4, 7). Its first value is at index 0 and its second at index 1, like a list. len(point) counts its values.

Tuples are immutable as containers. You can read point[0], but assigning point[0] = 9 raises TypeError. Choose a tuple for a fixed coordinate or color; choose a list when items need to be added, removed, or replaced.

The comma makes a tuple. (5) is the integer 5 in parentheses. (5,) is a one-item tuple. With several values, commas separate the items.

Immutability applies to the tuple's slots, not recursively to every object inside. If a tuple contains a list, that inner list can still be changed. The tuple continues to refer to the same list object.

terminology.definition: An ordered collection whose positions cannot be reassigned after creation.
A container whose stored positions cannot be replaced, added, or removed.
A tuple with one value; its comma is required, as in (5,).
An object whose contents can change, such as a list inside a tuple.

55.syntax_breakdown:
point = (4, 7)    # a two-item tuple
point[0]          # read first item
one = (5,)        # one-item tuple: comma is required
not_tuple = (5)   # just the integer 5 in parentheses

practical_examples.title: Store and read a coordinate
practical_examples.code:
point = (4, 7)
print(point[0])
print(point[1])
practical_examples.explanation: The tuple keeps x and y together in a fixed order. Index 0 is x and index 1 is y.

practical_examples.title: Make a one-item tuple
practical_examples.code:
choice = ('Start',)
print(choice)
print(len(choice))
practical_examples.explanation: The comma makes choice a tuple. len() confirms it contains one item.

practical_examples.title: An inner list can still change
practical_examples.code:
record = ('Mia', ['Python'])
record[1].append('Art')
print(record)
practical_examples.explanation: The tuple's second slot still points to the same list, but that list's contents can change.

line_by_line.explanation: Create a tuple with two coordinate values in order.
Read and display the value at index 0, which is 4.
Read and display the value at index 1, which is 7.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing one = (5) for a one-item tuple.
common_mistakes.why: Parentheses alone group the integer; they do not make a tuple.
common_mistakes.fix: Write one = (5,).

common_mistakes.mistake: Trying to assign point[0] = 9.
common_mistakes.why: Tuple positions cannot be reassigned.
common_mistakes.fix: Create a new tuple or use a list if the group must change.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a tuple containing a list freezes that list.
common_mistakes.why: The tuple slot is fixed, but the list object is mutable.
common_mistakes.fix: Remember the difference between changing a tuple slot and changing an inner object.

55.real_world_apps: Coordinates such as (x, y), screen sizes such as (width, height), and RGB colors are small fixed groups. A roster or inventory that changes is usually better stored in a list.
55.summary: Tuples keep ordered values in fixed positions. Read them by index, but do not reassign a position. A one-item tuple needs a comma. A tuple may contain a mutable object whose contents can still change.
practice_questions: What is point[1] for point = (8, 3)? Check: 3.
Which is a one-item tuple: (5) or (5,)? Check: (5,).
Should a changing shopping basket use a tuple or a list? Check: a list.
Can a list inside a tuple be changed? Check: yes; the tuple slot stays fixed, but the list is mutable.

56.title: Tuple Packing and Unpacking
learning_objectives: Pack values into a tuple, with or without parentheses.
Unpack values into variables in matching order.
Swap two values with multiple assignment.
Predict the error when value count and target count differ.
Unpack pairs in a for loop.
56.prerequisites: Know tuples, variables, and loops. Level 55 introduced fixed ordered groups; this lesson names tuple values as they are assigned.
56.introduction: A coordinate may arrive as a pair (4, 7), or a score report may contain a name and score. Instead of repeatedly reading positions, unpacking gives each value a clear variable name in one statement.
56.detailed_explanation:
Packing puts several values into one tuple. point = (4, 7) packs two values; point = 4, 7 also works because commas make a tuple.

Unpacking assigns tuple items to targets in order: x, y = point sends the first item to x and the second to y. There must be the same number of targets as values. If the counts differ, Python raises ValueError. Unpacking does not sort or search; it uses the existing order.

Multiple assignment is useful for swapping: left, right = right, left. Python evaluates the right-hand values before assigning them, so neither old value is lost.

A loop can unpack pairs too. In for name, score in records:, each record's first value goes to name and second to score. Use this when every item has the same shape and the order of each pair is meaningful.

terminology.definition: Putting several values together in a tuple.
Assigning tuple values to several variables in order.
A variable on the receiving side of an assignment.
One statement assigning multiple values, including a safe swap.
An error raised when unpacking gets a different number of values than targets.

56.syntax_breakdown:
point = (4, 7)          # pack
x, y = point            # unpack in order
left, right = right, left # swap
for name, score in records:
    print(name, score)  # unpack each pair

practical_examples.title: Pack and unpack a coordinate
practical_examples.code:
point = (4, 7)
x, y = point
print(x)
print(y)
practical_examples.explanation: The tuple contains two values. Unpacking assigns the first to x and the second to y.

practical_examples.title: Swap two values
practical_examples.code:
left = 'red'
right = 'blue'
left, right = right, left
print(left)
print(right)
practical_examples.explanation: Python evaluates the right side first, then assigns both results, so the old values exchange places.

practical_examples.title: Unpack pairs while looping
practical_examples.explanation: Each pair's first value goes to name and second goes to score on each loop pass.

line_by_line.explanation: Pack the two coordinate values into a tuple.
Unpack the first tuple value into x and the second into y.
Display the value that came from tuple position 0.
Display the value that came from tuple position 1.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing x, y = (4, 7, 9).
common_mistakes.why: There are three values but only two targets.
common_mistakes.fix: Make the number of targets match the number of values.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming unpacking sorts values.
common_mistakes.why: Unpacking follows the tuple's order.
common_mistakes.fix: Put values in the intended order or choose meaningful target names.

common_mistakes.mistake: Swapping with left = right, then right = left.
common_mistakes.why: The first assignment overwrites the old left value.
common_mistakes.fix: Use left, right = right, left.

56.real_world_apps: Unpack coordinate pairs, name-score records, and pairs returned by other code. It makes the role of each position clearer than repeating point[0] or point[1].
56.summary: Packing combines values into a tuple. Unpacking assigns values to targets in order, and their counts must match. Multiple assignment swaps safely. A loop can unpack each pair as it visits it.
practice_questions: After x, y = (12, 5), what is y? Check: 5.
Why does a, b = (1, 2, 3) fail? Check: there are three values but two targets.
Swap a and b in one statement. Check: a, b = b, a.
In for name, score in [('Ari', 90)], what goes into score? Check: 90, the pair's second value.

57.title: Introduction to Sets
learning_objectives: Create sets and explain how they remove duplicate values.
Test membership with in.
Explain why sets have no positional indexes or promised display order.
Create an empty set with set().
Recognize that set elements must be hashable.
57.prerequisites: Know lists and duplicates. A set is a collection chosen for uniqueness and membership, not positional access.
57.introduction: A game records tags a player has collected, but the same tag can arrive more than once. A list keeps every repeat. A set keeps one copy of each distinct value, so it is useful for unique tags and membership checks.
57.detailed_explanation:
A set stores unique hashable values. Braces can create one: tags = {'python', 'game'}. If a value appears twice, the set keeps one copy. Sets have no positional order, so tags[0] is invalid. Use a loop to visit items or sorted(tags) when you need a predictable display.

The in operator asks whether a value is present: 'python' in tags returns True or False. This is a direct way to check whether an item has already been collected.

Use set() for an empty set. Empty braces {} make an empty dictionary. Set elements must be hashable: strings and numbers are common examples. Lists can change, so they cannot be set elements; a tuple of hashable values can be.

Use a list when order or repeated items matter. Use a set when you need distinct values and membership checks. Never rely on the order in which a set prints; sort comparable items when order matters to a person.

terminology.definition: An unordered collection of unique hashable values.
Whether a value is present; test with value in collection.
A value suitable as a stable set element or dictionary key.
A set with no values, created with set(); {} creates an empty dictionary.

57.syntax_breakdown:
tags = {'python', 'game', 'python'} # duplicate kept once
'python' in tags                     # True or False
empty = set()                        # empty set
ordered = sorted(tags)               # predictable display
# Sets do not support tags[0].

practical_examples.title: Remove duplicates and check membership
practical_examples.code:
tags = {'python', 'game', 'python'}
print(sorted(tags))
print('python' in tags)
print('java' in tags)
practical_examples.explanation: The repeated value is kept once. sorted() makes an ordered list for display. in checks whether each word is present.

practical_examples.title: Create an empty set
practical_examples.code:
seen = set()
seen.add('map')
print('map' in seen)
print(len(seen))
practical_examples.explanation: set() creates an empty set; add() stores a value. {} would create a dictionary instead.

practical_examples.title: Use a tuple as a set element
practical_examples.code:
locations = {('x', 3), ('y', 4)}
print(len(locations))
practical_examples.explanation: The tuples contain hashable strings and numbers, so they can be set elements. A list cannot be used because it is mutable.

line_by_line.explanation: Create a set; the repeated python value does not make a second copy.
Sort the distinct values so their displayed order is predictable.
Check whether python belongs to the set; this is True.
Check an absent value; this is False.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing empty = {} for an empty set.
common_mistakes.why: Python uses {} for an empty dictionary.
common_mistakes.fix: Write empty = set().

common_mistakes.mistake: Trying tags[0].
common_mistakes.why: Sets do not have a positional order or indexes.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a loop to visit values or sorted(tags) to display them in order.

common_mistakes.mistake: Expecting a set to preserve the typed order.
common_mistakes.why: A set is not an ordered sequence.
common_mistakes.fix: Sort comparable items when display order matters.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding a list to a set.
common_mistakes.why: Lists are mutable and unhashable.
common_mistakes.fix: Use individual hashable values or a tuple of hashable values.

57.real_world_apps: A set can track unique course tags, product labels, or visited pages. Membership can check whether an item has already been collected. Use a list instead if order or repeats matter.
57.summary: Sets remove duplicates and support membership checks with in. They have no indexes or guaranteed order. Use set() for an empty set. Values must be hashable; sorted() gives predictable display for comparable values.
practice_questions: How many values are in {2, 2, 5}? Check: 2.
What does {} create? Check: an empty dictionary, not a set.
What does 'key' in items return? Check: True or False.
Why can a tuple be in a set while a list cannot? Check: a list can change and is unhashable.

58.title: Set Operations (Union, Intersection, Difference)
learning_objectives: Use | for union and & for intersection.
Use - for directional difference and ^ for symmetric difference.
Explain which values each operation keeps.
Sort results for predictable display.
58.prerequisites: Know that sets keep unique values and have no indexes. Level 57 introduced set creation and membership.
58.introduction: Two friends have game items. You may want everything they own, only the shared items, items only one friend owns, or items owned by exactly one friend. Set operations express each question directly.
58.detailed_explanation:
Let A = {'red', 'blue'} and B = {'blue', 'green'}. Union, A | B, combines values from either set and keeps each once. Intersection, A & B, keeps only values in both. Difference, A - B, keeps values in A that are not in B. Difference is directional: A - B can differ from B - A.

Symmetric difference, A ^ B, keeps values that appear in one set but not both. In this example, red and green remain; shared blue is excluded. Each operator returns a new set and leaves the original sets unchanged.

Sets do not promise display order. sorted(result) returns a list in a predictable order when values can be compared. Choose by the question: everything means |; shared means &; from the first group only means -; in one group but not both means ^. Reading the operation in plain words prevents confusing difference with symmetric difference.

terminology.definition: All distinct values from either set.
Only values found in both sets.
Values in the left set but not the right; direction matters.
Values in exactly one set, excluding shared values.
Returns an ordered list for predictable display.

58.syntax_breakdown:
A | B # union: all values from either
A & B # intersection: only shared values
A - B # in A, not in B
A ^ B # in one set, not both
sorted(A | B) # sort the result for display

practical_examples.title: Compare two groups with all four operations
practical_examples.explanation: Union returns all colors. Intersection returns shared blue. Difference keeps red from a. Symmetric difference keeps red and green, which occur in exactly one set.

practical_examples.title: Difference depends on operand order
practical_examples.explanation: A - B asks for values in a but not b. B - A asks the reverse question.

practical_examples.title: Union keeps a shared item once
practical_examples.explanation: key occurs in both sets, but a set contains only one copy.

line_by_line.explanation: Create the first group.
Create the second group; blue is shared.
Combine all values, then sort the result for display.
Keep only values present in both sets.
Keep values from a that are absent from b.
Keep values present in one set but not both.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using A - B to combine two groups.
common_mistakes.why: Minus keeps only values from the left that are absent on the right.
common_mistakes.fix: Use A | B for union.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming A - B equals B - A.
common_mistakes.why: Difference starts with the left set, so order changes the question.
common_mistakes.fix: Read A - B as 'in A but not in B.'

common_mistakes.mistake: Using ^ for shared values.
common_mistakes.why: Symmetric difference excludes values in both sets.
common_mistakes.fix: Use & for the intersection.

common_mistakes.mistake: Expecting raw set output to be alphabetic.
common_mistakes.why: Sets do not guarantee display order.
common_mistakes.fix: Use sorted(result) when a predictable order matters.

58.real_world_apps: Compare course registrations to find all offered courses, courses two students share, courses only one student has, or courses taken by exactly one student. Choose the operator from the question being asked.
58.summary: Use | for union, & for intersection, - for left-side difference, and ^ for symmetric difference. Operations return new sets. Use sorted() for predictable display; A - B is directional.
practice_questions: Which operator keeps only shared values? Check: &.
If A = {1, 2} and B = {2, 3}, what is A - B? Check: {1}.
Which operator keeps values in one set but not both? Check: ^.
Why sort a set result before displaying it? Check: sets do not promise a predictable order.

59.title: Introduction to Dictionaries
learning_objectives: Create a dictionary of key-value pairs and retrieve a value by key.
Add a new pair or update the value under an existing key.
Explain unique keys and the hashable-key requirement.
Predict the result of looking up a missing key with brackets.
Choose a dictionary for labeled information rather than numbered positions.
59.prerequisites: Know variables, strings, numbers, and lists. A dictionary connects each value to a meaningful label such as name, level, or score.
59.introduction: A student record may contain a name, class, and score. Separate numbered positions are hard to remember. A dictionary labels each value, so code can ask for the score by its key instead of remembering its position.
59.detailed_explanation:
A dictionary maps keys to values. Write pairs inside braces: hero = {'name': 'Mia', 'level': 3}. The key 'name' labels Mia; 'level' labels 3. A colon separates key and value, and commas separate pairs.

Use hero['name'] to retrieve Mia. Assignment adds or updates: hero['level'] = 4 changes an existing value; hero['class'] = 'Ranger' creates a new pair. Keys are unique, so assigning to an existing key replaces its old value. Values may repeat.

Keys must be hashable. Strings and numbers are common keys; lists are mutable and cannot be keys. Looking up a missing key with brackets raises KeyError. Level 60 introduces get() for cases where a key may be absent.

Dictionaries preserve insertion order in modern Python, but use them as mappings rather than numbered sequences. A list is better for an ordered group of repeated records; each record can be a dictionary so its fields are labeled.

terminology.definition: A mapping that connects keys to values.
A unique, hashable label used to retrieve a value.
The information stored under a key.
A label and the information connected to it.
An error from bracket lookup when a key is absent.

59.syntax_breakdown:
hero = {'name': 'Mia', 'level': 3}
hero['name']             # retrieve a value
hero['level'] = 4        # update a value
hero['class'] = 'Ranger' # add a new pair
# hero['score'] raises KeyError if score is missing

practical_examples.title: Read, update, and add details
practical_examples.code:
hero = {'name': 'Mia', 'level': 3}
print(hero['name'])
hero['level'] = 4
hero['class'] = 'Ranger'
print(hero)
practical_examples.explanation: The name key retrieves Mia. The level assignment updates an existing pair; class adds a new pair.

practical_examples.title: A repeated key updates its value
practical_examples.explanation: A dictionary cannot keep two separate values for one key. The new assignment replaces the old value.

practical_examples.title: Use a meaningful label
practical_examples.code:
scores = {'math': 91, 'art': 86}
print(scores['art'])
practical_examples.explanation: The label art retrieves its score. No position number has to be remembered.

line_by_line.explanation: Create two key-value pairs in a dictionary.
Look up the value connected to name and display Mia.
Replace the value under the existing level key.
Add class because that key was not present.
Display the dictionary after the update and addition.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing hero[name] when name is the literal key text.
common_mistakes.why: Without quotes Python looks for a variable called name.
common_mistakes.fix: Write hero['name'].

common_mistakes.mistake: Expecting a missing bracket lookup to return an empty value.
common_mistakes.why: A missing key raises KeyError.
common_mistakes.fix: Use get() when the key may be absent and a fallback is appropriate.

common_mistakes.mistake: Expecting another copy of a key when assigning it again.
common_mistakes.why: Keys are unique; the new value replaces the old one.
common_mistakes.fix: Store several values in a list under one key if that is the intended structure.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a list as a key.
common_mistakes.why: Lists can change and are unhashable.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a string, number, or suitable tuple as a key.

59.real_world_apps: A settings dictionary can map volume to 8 and language to English. A student record can map name to Mia and score to 91. Dictionaries fit information retrieved by meaningful labels.
59.summary: Dictionaries map unique, hashable keys to values. Brackets retrieve, add, or update values; a missing key raises KeyError. Choose dictionaries for labeled information and lists for ordered sequences.
practice_questions: What does player['level'] return for {'level': 4}? Check: 4.
What happens when assigning to an existing key? Check: its value is replaced.
Why might scores['history'] raise KeyError? Check: history may not exist.
Choose a list or dictionary for one score under each subject name. Check: dictionary, because subjects are labels.

60.title: Essential Dictionary Methods
learning_objectives: Use get() to return a fallback for a missing key without changing the dictionary.
Visit keys, values, or key-value pairs with dictionary methods.
Unpack each pair from items() inside a loop.
Use update() and pop() and understand their side effects and return values.
Choose brackets or get() based on whether a key must exist.
60.prerequisites: Know how to create, retrieve, and update dictionary entries. Level 59 explained that a missing bracket lookup raises KeyError.
60.introduction: A settings screen may need to show a theme even when the user has never chosen one. The program needs a safe fallback. Dictionary methods help with missing keys and with processing many stored labels and values.
60.detailed_explanation:
get(key, default) returns the value when a key exists. If it is missing, get() returns the supplied default instead of raising KeyError. With no default it returns None. get() does not add the missing key; assign with brackets when you want to create it.

keys() gives the keys, values() gives the values, and items() gives key-value pairs. A loop can unpack those pairs: for subject, score in scores.items():. Each pair's first value goes to subject and the second to score. Iteration follows dictionary insertion order.

update(other) adds new pairs or replaces values for matching keys. It changes the original dictionary and returns None. pop(key) removes a pair and returns its value. You can pass a fallback to pop() for a missing key. Save pop()'s return when it matters; do not assign update()'s return to the dictionary.

Use bracket lookup when the key is required and a missing key is a real problem. Use get() when absence is normal and the program should continue with a useful fallback.

terminology.definition: Returns a present value or a fallback when the key is missing; does not insert the fallback.
Provides key-value pairs for iteration.
Provide the dictionary's keys or values for iteration.
Adds or replaces pairs in place and returns None.
Removes a key and returns its value.

60.syntax_breakdown:
theme = settings.get('theme', 'light')
for key, value in settings.items():
    print(key, value)
settings.update({'volume': 8}) # changes settings; returns None
old = settings.pop('theme', 'light') # remove; fallback if absent

practical_examples.title: Safely read an optional setting
practical_examples.code:
settings = {'volume': 8}
theme = settings.get('theme', 'light')
print(theme)
print(settings)
practical_examples.explanation: theme is absent, so get() returns light. It does not insert theme into settings.

practical_examples.title: Visit each key-value pair
practical_examples.explanation: items() supplies pairs. The loop unpacks each pair into subject and score.

practical_examples.title: Update a value and remove another
practical_examples.code:
settings = {'volume': 5, 'theme': 'dark'}
settings.update({'volume': 8})
old_theme = settings.pop('theme')
print(old_theme)
print(settings)
practical_examples.explanation: update() changes volume. pop() removes theme and returns dark, which is saved in old_theme.

line_by_line.explanation: Create a dictionary with volume but no theme key.
Ask for theme; because it is absent, get() returns light rather than raising KeyError.
Display the fallback returned by get().
Show that get() did not add theme to the dictionary.

common_mistakes.mistake: Thinking get() adds its fallback to the dictionary.
common_mistakes.why: get() returns a value but does not change the mapping.
common_mistakes.fix: Use settings[key] = value when you want to add a key.

common_mistakes.mistake: Looping over a dictionary directly and expecting pairs.
common_mistakes.why: A direct dictionary loop visits keys only.
common_mistakes.fix: Use for key, value in settings.items() when both values are needed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing settings = settings.update(other).
common_mistakes.why: update() changes the dictionary and returns None.
common_mistakes.fix: Call settings.update(other) without assignment.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using brackets for an optional key.
common_mistakes.why: A missing key raises KeyError.
common_mistakes.fix: Use get(key, fallback) when absence is expected.

60.real_world_apps: A game can read an optional sound setting with a default. A report can print every setting using items(). A program can update configuration or remove a temporary entry after use.

61.title: Nested Collections (2D Data & JSON Models)
learning_objectives: Read a cell from a list of lists one level at a time.
Read a field from a dictionary inside a list.
Explain the job of each nested layer.

61.prerequisites: Know lists, indexes, dictionaries, and keys. A nested collection stores a familiar list or dictionary inside another collection.
61.introduction: A game board has rows and columns, while a class roster has records with names and scores. One flat sequence cannot clearly represent all of these layers. Nested collections keep related groups together and let you select one level at a time.
61.detailed_explanation:
A nested collection contains another collection as an item. A grid can be a list of lists: grid = [['A', 'B'], ['C', 'D']]. The outer list stores rows; each inner list stores its cells. To get B, Python first evaluates grid[0] and gets ['A', 'B']; then [1] selects B. So grid[0][1] means first row, second cell.

A list of dictionaries stores ordered records. In students[0]['name'], the first bracket selects the first dictionary; the second asks that dictionary for the value under name. Read from the outside inward and keep track of what each expression returns.

Lists are useful for ordered groups; dictionaries label the fields in a record. Nested structures combine those jobs. JSON is a text format for exchanging data. It resembles Python lists and dictionaries, but JSON text is not itself a Python dictionary; it must be parsed into Python values before normal dictionary access.

An inner list is still mutable. Changing it changes the object stored inside the outer list. When a nested expression looks confusing, evaluate one bracket at a time and name the intermediate row or record.

A list of row lists; one index selects a row and another selects a cell.

62.title: Iterating Over Collections (enumerate & zip)
learning_objectives: Use a for loop to visit each item.
Use enumerate() to receive both an item and its count.
Set enumerate()'s starting count with start=.
Use zip() to pair values at matching positions and unpack the pair.
Explain that zip() stops at the shortest input and does not check equal lengths.
62.prerequisites: Know lists, for loops, and tuple unpacking. Level 56 explained how two values can be assigned to two loop variables.
62.introduction: A menu needs numbers beside each choice, and a report needs to match each person with a score. A loop can visit items, but manual counters and indexes can be easy to misalign. enumerate() and zip() provide the needed pairs as the loop runs.
62.detailed_explanation:
A for loop visits items one by one. enumerate(items) pairs each item with a count: by default the first count is 0. Use enumerate(items, start=1) when people expect numbering to begin at 1. The loop can unpack each pair: for number, choice in enumerate(choices, start=1):.

zip(names, scores) pairs values by position: first name with first score, second with second, and so on. for name, score in zip(names, scores): unpacks each pair. The lists must be in corresponding order for the pairing to make sense.

zip() stops when the shortest input runs out. If there are three names and two scores, it makes two pairs and leaves the extra name unused. It does not warn or raise an error. Compare lengths first if equal counts are required.

Use enumerate when one collection needs a count. Use zip when separate collections contain matching values in the same order. If the order is not trustworthy, keep related values together in records instead of pairing by position.

63.title: World 6 Examination & Capstone: Student Records Management System
learning_objectives: Design a student record as a dictionary with meaningful keys.
Store many records in a list and retrieve nested values from the outside inward.
Update a student's score and calculate an average using sum() and len().
Collect unique course names in a set and sort them for display.
Use enumerate() and f-strings to print a numbered report.
Explain why each collection fits its job and distinguish Python data from JSON text.
63.prerequisites: This project uses strings, lists, tuples, sets, dictionaries, nested access, loops, enumerate(), and f-strings from World 6, plus basic addition, division, sum(), and len(). The steps recap each tool as it appears.
63.introduction: A teacher wants a small program that stores several student records, adds a score, finds all courses taught, and prints a readable report. Different parts of the information have different needs: students stay in order, each student's fields need labels, scores and courses can contain several values, and course names should be unique in the final catalog. This capstone combines the right collection for each job.
63.detailed_explanation:
Plan the shape of the data first. One student record is a dictionary: the key 'name' labels the student's name, 'scores' labels a list of scores, and 'courses' labels a list of course names. The outer students list stores several records in order. Each structure has one job: a list keeps an ordered group; a dictionary makes fields readable by name; a set removes duplicate course names.

Stage 1: Read one nested value. students[0] selects the first dictionary from the outer list. students[0]['name'] then selects that dictionary's name. Read one bracket at a time to avoid mixing up the outer list index and inner dictionary key.

Stage 2: Update a record. students[0]['scores'] reaches Mia's score list. append(96) changes that list by adding one score. The record is a dictionary, and its scores value is a list, so the nested access follows those two layers.

Stage 3: Collect unique courses. set() creates an empty set. The nested loops visit each student and then each course in that student's course list. add(course) stores each course; if Art appears again, the set still keeps one Art. A set has no display order, so sorted(all_courses) creates a predictable ordered list for the report.

Stage 4: Calculate and report. enumerate(students, start=1) pairs each student with a count for the printed report. sum(scores) adds the numbers; len(scores) counts them; dividing the total by the count gives the average. The program stores intermediate values in names so the final f-string stays readable. The .1f format displays one digit after the decimal; it does not change the average variable. join() combines course names with comma-space separators.

The complete program stays in memory. It does not save a file or connect to a database. The dictionaries and lists are Python objects, not JSON text. A real student system would need input checks, saved storage, privacy protection, and access controls; those topics are beyond World 6. The small program here teaches how collections can fit together to solve one coherent problem.

terminology.definition: A dictionary describing one student with labeled fields.
A list or dictionary stored inside another collection.
A course name included once even if several students take it.
The sum of scores divided by the number of scores.

A text format for exchanging structured data; it is different from the live Python dictionaries used here.

practical_examples.title: Complete project: Student Records Management System
practical_examples.code:
students = [
    {'name': 'Mia', 'scores': [88, 92], 'courses': ['Python', 'Art']},
    {'name': 'Kai', 'scores': [75, 85], 'courses': ['Art', 'Science']}
]

# Add a new score to Mia's existing scores list.
students[0]['scores'].append(96)

# Gather course names; the set keeps each course only once.
all_courses = set()
for student in students:
    for course in student['courses']:
        all_courses.add(course)

print('Unique courses:', sorted(all_courses))
print('Student report:')
for number, student in enumerate(students, start=1):
    scores = student['scores']
    average = sum(scores) / len(scores)
    name = student['name']
    course_text = ', '.join(student['courses'])
    print(f'{number}. {name} - Average: {average:.1f}')
    print(f'   Courses: {course_text}')
practical_examples.explanation: The outer list keeps students ordered. Each dictionary labels one record's fields. Scores and courses are inner lists because one student can have several. The first nested assignment adds a score to Mia. The nested loops gather each course into a set, removing repeats. sorted() makes course output predictable. The final loop numbers each student, calculates the average, joins course names, and formats each line.

106.title: List, Dict, and Set Comprehensions
106.learning_objectives: ["Construct list comprehensions with transformation expressions and filtering conditions", "Build dictionary comprehensions {k: v for ...} and set comprehensions {x for ...}", "Understand how comprehensions run faster in C-bytecode than equivalent append loops"]
106.introduction: In Python, creating a new list by transforming or filtering an existing one using an explicit 5-line `for` loop with `.append()` is considered unpythonic. Python provides comprehensions — a concise, declarative syntax that expresses the entire operation in a single elegant line that runs faster in C-bytecode.
106.detailed_explanation:
List Comprehensions (Turbo Builders):

1. `⚡ The 1-Line Superpower`: Turns 4 lines of `squares = []; for ... append()` into 1 elegant, high-speed line!
2. `🏭 Transform on Left`: What you want in the new list goes first: `[name.upper() for name in names]`.
3. `🧹 Filter on Right`: Append `if x > 0` at the very end to filter out negative numbers or junk.
106.terminology: [{"term": "List Comprehension", "definition": "⚡ Turbo Builder: A lightning-fast, one-line syntax to build a brand new list from an existing one: [x*2 for x in nums]."}, {"term": "[expression for item in iterable]", "definition": "📐 Comprehension Blueprint: The transform formula on the left, loop in the middle, and optional 'if' filter on the right."}, {"term": "Filter Comprehension", "definition": "🧹 Instant Filter: Adding 'if x > 0' at the end to keep only matching items."}]

# squares = []
# for x in range(5):
#     squares.append(x ** 2)

# Modern 1-line Turbo Builder:

evens = [n for n in range(10) if n % 2 == 0]
print('Squares:', squares) # [0, 1, 4, 9, 16]
print('Evens:', evens)     # [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]

107.title: Iterators and the Iteration Protocol
107.learning_objectives: ["Distinguish between an Iterable and an Iterator", "Manually advance iterators using iter() and next()", "Understand how for loops intercept StopIteration behind the scenes"]
107.prerequisites: Level 106: List, Dict, and Set Comprehensions
107.introduction: When you write `for item in sequence:`, what is Python actually doing behind the scenes? It doesn't use a numeric index counter! Python uses the universal Iteration Protocol: converting the collection into an Iterator and pulling items one by one with `next()`.
107.detailed_explanation:
Iterators and the Iteration Protocol:

1. `🍬 The Pez Dispenser Analogy`: Instead of dumping 1,000,000 candies on the floor, an iterator keeps them in a stack and hands you one candy at a time when you press `next()`.
2. `🔄 How Loops Work Behind the Scenes`: Every time you write `for item in items:`, Python secretly calls `iter()` and `next()` under the hood!
3. `🛑 StopIteration`: Python's silent signal that says 'we reached the end of the collection!'.
107.terminology: [{"term": "Iterator", "definition": "🍬 Pez Candy Dispenser: An object in memory that produces the next item one-by-one whenever you call next()."}, {"term": "iter()", "definition": "🔄 Load Dispenser: Turns any list or collection into an active iterator object."}, {"term": "next()", "definition": "👇 Dispense One: Pushes out the very next item waiting in line."}, {"term": "StopIteration", "definition": "🛑 Empty Dispenser: The signal Python raises when the iterator has no more items left."}]

print(next(dispenser)) # 'Apple'

        curr = self.val
        self.val -= 1
        return curr

108.title: Generators and the yield Keyword
108.learning_objectives: ["Define generator functions using the yield keyword", "Understand execution pausing and resumption in generators", "Leverage lazy evaluation to process massive data with near-zero memory footprint"]
108.prerequisites: Level 107: Iterators and the Iteration Protocol
108.introduction: What if you need to calculate the first 10,000,000 Fibonacci numbers? Generating a list of 10 million numbers requires gigabytes of RAM and takes seconds to compute before you can even look at the first number. A Generator creates numbers on demand, one at a time, consuming virtually zero memory!
108.detailed_explanation:
Generators & The `yield` Keyword:

1. `⏸️ yield vs return`: `return` finishes the function and destroys its state. `yield` pauses the function like a movie, hands you the value, and freezes until you ask for the next one!
2. `🪶 Saving Gigabytes of RAM`: If you generate 100,000,000 rows from a database, a normal list would crash your computer out of memory. A generator yields 1 row at a time with 0 lag!
3. `✨ Lazy Evaluation`: Calculates values ONLY when requested.

When called again, it resumes right where it paused!"}, {"term": "Memory Efficiency", "definition": "🪶 Feather Light: Can generate 1,000,000,000 numbers while using almost ZERO megabytes of computer RAM."}]

109.title: Generator Expressions vs List Comprehensions
109.learning_objectives: ["Construct generator expressions using parentheses: (x for x in iterable)", "Compare memory usage between eager list comprehensions and lazy generator expressions using sys.getsizeof()", "Pass generator expressions directly into aggregators like sum(), min(), max()"]
109.prerequisites: Level 108: Generators and the yield Keyword
109.introduction: Did you know that changing square brackets `[]` to parentheses `()` turns a list comprehension into a generator expression? This simple syntax difference can reduce your program's memory consumption from 800 Megabytes down to 100 Bytes!
109.detailed_explanation:
Generator Expressions vs List Comprehensions:

1. `[] vs ()`: Square brackets `[]` build a full list in memory right now. Round parentheses `()` build a streaming generator pipeline.
2. `⚡ Huge Sums in 1 Line`: `sum(x for x in range(1000000))` computes the sum without ever creating a giant 1,000,000-item list in RAM!
3. `💡 Rule of Thumb`: If you need to index `[0]` or slice `[:]`, use a list. If you just need to loop through once or sum, use a generator!
109.terminology: [{"term": "Generator Expression ( )", "definition": "🪶 Feather Stream: Looks like a list comprehension but wrapped in round parentheses `()` instead of brackets `[]`."}, {"term": "Stream vs Memory", "definition": "🌊 River vs 🏊 Pool: A list comprehension holds the entire pool of water in RAM; a generator expression is a flowing river that passes one drop at a time."}]
109.syntax_breakdown:
# List comp (Stores all in RAM):
list_squares = [x**2 for x in range(1000)]

# GenExpr (Feather light stream, zero RAM):
gen_squares = (x**2 for x in range(1000))
print('First item from generator stream:', next(gen_squares)) # 0
print('Second item:', next(gen_squares))                     # 1

110.title: Closures and First-Class Functions
110.learning_objectives: ["Understand nested (inner) functions", "Understand what a Closure is in Python (a function retaining its enclosing scope)", "Inspect captured closure state using __closure__ and cell_contents"]
110.prerequisites: Level 109: Generator Expressions vs List Comprehensions
110.introduction: Can a function remember a variable even after the outer function that created it has completely finished running and exited? Yes! In Python, this phenomenon is called a Closure. Closures are the conceptual foundation of decorators.
110.detailed_explanation:
Closures & First-Class Functions:

1. `🎫 Functions are Values`: You can do `my_tool = print` and then type `my_tool('Hello')`!
2. `🎒 The Closure Memory Backpack`: Notice how `double(5)` remembers that `factor` was `2`, even though `make_multiplier` already finished 10 minutes ago!
3. `🏗️ Foundation of Decorators`: Closures are the secret engine behind Python decorators.
110.terminology: [{"term": "First-Class Function", "definition": "🎫 VIP Citizen: In Python, functions are regular objects! You can pass a function into another function, store it in a variable, or put it in a list."}, {"term": "Closure", "definition": "🎒 Memory Backpack: An inner function that remembers the variables from its outer function even after the outer function has finished running!"}]
110.syntax_breakdown:
# Function returning another function with memory (Closure):
def make_multiplier(factor):
    def multiply(x):
        return x * factor   # Remembers 'factor' forever!
    return multiply

double = make_multiplier(2)
triple = make_multiplier(3)
print('Double 5:', double(5)) # 10
print('Triple 5:', triple(5)) # 15

111.title: Function Decorators (@decorator syntax)
111.learning_objectives: ["Understand decorators as higher-order functions wrapping target functions", "Use the @decorator syntactic sugar", "Preserve function metadata (name, docstring) using functools.wraps"]
111.introduction: What if you need to measure the execution time of 20 different functions, or ensure that only logged-in users can access 15 web routes? Copy-pasting timing or authentication code into every single function creates bloated, unmaintainable code. Decorators let you wrap existing functions with reusable behavior in a single line: `@my_decorator`.
111.detailed_explanation:
Function Decorators (`@decorator`):

1. `🎁 The Gift Wrapping Analogy`: You have a toy (the function). A decorator wraps the toy in wrapping paper (extra code before and after) without changing how the toy itself works!
2. `⏱️ Real-World Uses`: Used everywhere in Python for measuring execution speed, checking if a user is logged in, and rate limiting.
3. `🎀 The @ Sugar`: Writing `@announce` above `def launch():` is a clean shortcut for `launch = announce(launch)`.
111.terminology: [{"term": "Decorator (@syntax)", "definition": "🎁 Gift Wrapping: A function that wraps another function to add extra superpowers (like logging, timing, or security checks) without modifying the original function's code!"}, {"term": "@decorator", "definition": "🎀 The Bow on Top: Placing @my_decorator directly above a function definition to wrap it automatically."}]

111.summary: Decorators wrap functions with reusable pre/post behavior using @decorator. Always use @wraps(func) to preserve metadata.

112.title: Decorators with Arguments
112.learning_objectives: ["Understand why decorators with arguments require a 3-tier nested architecture", "Build parameterized decorators like @repeat(num_times=3)", "Understand how decorator factories work"]
112.introduction: What if you want to configure your decorator — for instance, specifying how many times to retry an API call `@retry(max_attempts=3)` or setting a rate limit `@rate_limit(calls=60)`? Because you are passing arguments to the decorator itself, you need a Decorator Factory.
112.detailed_explanation:
Decorators with Arguments:

1. `🎛️ Adjustable Dials`: Adding parameters like `@retry(attempts=3)` lets you customize how the wrapper operates.
2. `🏗️ The 3-Tier Layer`: An outer function receives the decorator settings, the middle function receives the target function, and the inner wrapper runs the code.
3. `🏷️ Always Use @wraps`: Protects `__name__` and documentation metadata.

113.title: Recursion and the Call Stack
113.learning_objectives: ["Understand how a function can call itself (Recursion)", "Identify the two mandatory components: Base Case and Recursive Step", "Understand the call stack and prevent RecursionError (Stack Overflow)"]
113.introduction: To understand recursion, you must first understand recursion! In computer science, recursion is an elegant technique where a function solves a problem by breaking it down into smaller instances of the exact same problem until it reaches a trivial baseline.
113.detailed_explanation:
Understanding Recursion:

1. `🪞 The Russian Nesting Doll Analogy`: You open a big doll, and inside is a smaller doll, and inside that is an even smaller doll until you reach the tiny solid doll (the Base Case)!
2. `🛑 Base Case is Mandatory`: Without a base case, the function calls itself forever until Python crashes with a `RecursionError`!
3. `🌲 Perfect for Trees & Folders`: Essential for traversing nested folder structures or binary search trees.
113.terminology: [{"term": "Recursion", "definition": "🪞 Hall of Mirrors: A function that solves a problem by calling ITSELF with a smaller piece of the problem until it hits a base case."}, {"term": "Base Case", "definition": "🛑 Emergency Stop Sign: The simple condition where the function stops calling itself and returns a direct answer (e.g. if n <= 1: return 1)."}, {"term": "Call Stack", "definition": "🥞 Stack of Pancakes: The memory stack where Python stores each recursive call while waiting for answers from below."}]
113.syntax_breakdown:
def countdown_recursive(n):
    # 1. Base Case (Stop Sign):
    if n <= 0:
        print('🚀 BLAST OFF!')
        return
    # 2. Recursive Step (Calling self with n - 1):
    print(n)
    countdown_recursive(n - 1)

countdown_recursive(3)

113.common_mistakes: [{"fix": "Always verify your base case executes and your recursive argument shrinks.", "mistake": "RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded", "why": "Missing base case or recursive step does not make progress toward the base case."}]
113.real_world_apps: Navigating nested directory filesystems, parsing JSON/XML hierarchical AST trees, divide-and-conquer algorithms (QuickSort, MergeSort).
113.summary: Recursion requires a base case to terminate and a recursive step moving toward the base case. Avoid unbounded recursion to prevent stack overflow.
113.practice_questions: ["What two components must every recursive function have?", "What error occurs if a recursive function lacks a base case?"]

114.title: Regular Expressions (re module)
114.learning_objectives: ["Understand regular expressions (regex) syntax and special characters (\\d, \\w, +, *, ?)", "Search and match patterns using re.search(), re.match(), and re.findall()", "Substitute and clean text patterns using re.sub()"]
114.prerequisites: Level 113: Recursion and the Call Stack
114.introduction: How do you validate that an email address has a valid domain, extract every phone number from a 500-page document, or redact credit card numbers? Standard string methods like `.find()` or `.split()` are completely inadequate for complex pattern matching. Regular Expressions (regex) provide a mini-language for text patterns.
114.detailed_explanation:
Regular Expressions (`re` Module):

1. `🔍 The Super Search Pattern`: Instead of writing 20 lines of string checks to validate an email, regex checks the entire format in 1 line!
2. `🔣 Core Cheat Sheet`: `\d` = digit, `\w` = letter/number, `+` = one or more, `*` = zero or more.
3. `🎣 re.findall()`: Scrapes all matching patterns out of long documents or websites automatically.
114.terminology: [{"term": "re (Regular Expressions)", "definition": "🔍 Super-Powered Search Filter: A special pattern language used to match text formats like emails, phone numbers, or zip codes in an instant."}, {"term": "re.findall(pattern, text)", "definition": "🎣 Catch All: Finds every occurrence matching the pattern and returns them in a list."}, {"term": "Regex Symbols", "definition": "🔣 Pattern Symbols: \\d means any digit (0-9), \\w means word character, + means one or more, and ^ means start of line."}]

import re

# Validate email pattern:

print('Is email valid?', is_valid) # True

116.title: Working with APIs and HTTP Requests
116.learning_objectives: ["Explain how a client asks a server for something.", "Choose GET, POST, PUT, or DELETE for a requested action.", "Read common HTTP status-code groups."]
116.introduction: When you open a page, your browser asks another computer for information. The server sends back the information or a short code explaining what happened.
116.detailed_explanation:
A client is the program that asks for something. A server receives the request and sends a reply. A browser is often a client, and the website is often the server.

The HTTP method says what the client wants: GET reads information, POST sends new information, PUT updates information, and DELETE removes information.

The status code tells how the request went. Codes 200–299 mean success. Codes 400–499 mean the request has a problem, such as a missing page. Codes 500–599 mean the server has a problem. This level practices sorting those replies with Python choices; the example does not contact the internet.

117.title: Consuming REST APIs in Python
117.learning_objectives: ["Read JSON text returned by a web service.", "Use json.loads() to turn JSON text into Python data.", "Check for a successful status before using response fields."]
117.prerequisites: Level 116: Working with APIs and HTTP Requests
117.introduction: A web service often sends its answer as JSON text. Python can turn that text into dictionaries and lists so your program can use the values.
117.detailed_explanation:
An API lets one program ask another program for information or an action. The reply has a status code and a response body. The body is the returned data.

JSON is a common text format for that data. It can contain names, values, lists, and nested objects. json.loads(text) reads the text and creates normal Python dictionaries, lists, numbers, and strings.

Check the status before reading fields such as title or data. A successful reply might include those fields; an error reply might contain something different. Our examples use saved sample replies, so they practice handling responses without making a real internet request.

118.title: Relational Databases and SQL Fundamentals
118.learning_objectives: ["Tell database tables, rows, and columns apart.", "Explain why each row needs a primary key.", "Recognize SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE."]
118.prerequisites: Level 117: Consuming REST APIs in Python
118.introduction: A database table is like a classroom roster. Each row is one person, and each column is one detail such as a name or score.
118.detailed_explanation:
A relational database stores related information in tables. A row is one complete record. A column is one kind of detail shared by all records. In a students table, name and score can be columns; one student's name and score make one row.

A primary key is a value that identifies one row, like a student number. Two students may share a name, but their IDs are different. Column types such as INTEGER, TEXT, and REAL describe the kind of value stored.

SQL is the language used to work with tables. SELECT reads rows, INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes rows, and DELETE removes rows. WHERE limits which rows are affected. Without WHERE, an update or delete can affect every row. The first example below prints SQL text; it does not run a database yet.

119.title: SQLite in Python: Connecting and Creating Tables
119.learning_objectives: ["Import Python's built-in sqlite3 library.", "Open a temporary database with sqlite3.connect(':memory:').", "Create a table and inspect its name."]
119.prerequisites: Level 118: Relational Databases and SQL Fundamentals
119.introduction: Now we will use a real database. We keep it in memory so it disappears when the program ends and leaves no practice files behind.
119.detailed_explanation:
sqlite3 is Python's built-in tool for SQLite databases. Import it, then call sqlite3.connect(':memory:') to open a temporary database in memory.

The connection is the open link to the database. A cursor sends SQL commands and reads their answers. You can also call connection.execute() for a short command. CREATE TABLE makes a table and lists its column names and types.

SQLite keeps a catalog named sqlite_master that describes tables. A SELECT query can ask that catalog whether your table exists. When finished, close the connection. For a database saved to disk, save changes with commit() before closing.

connection = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
connection.execute('CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER, name TEXT)')
rows = connection.execute("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table'").fetchall()
connection.close()

120.title: SQLite in Python: CRUD Operations
120.learning_objectives: ["Add rows with INSERT and read them with SELECT.", "Change or remove selected rows with UPDATE and DELETE.", "Use fetchone() for one row and fetchall() for a list of rows."]
120.prerequisites: Level 119: SQLite in Python: Connecting and Creating Tables
120.introduction: A game inventory changes as you play: you add an item, look at your items, change a count, or remove something. Those four actions are called CRUD.
120.detailed_explanation:
CRUD means Create, Read, Update, and Delete. INSERT adds a row. SELECT reads rows. UPDATE changes existing rows. DELETE removes rows.

A query can return one row or many rows. fetchone() gives one row as a tuple. fetchall() gives a list of all remaining rows. Use a loop to display each row in that list.

Use WHERE to choose which row to change. If you leave WHERE off UPDATE or DELETE, SQLite may change or remove every row. Use question-mark placeholders for user values; the next lesson explains why they are safer.
120.terminology: [{"term": "CRUD", "definition": "Create, Read, Update, and Delete."}, {"term": "INSERT", "definition": "Add a new row."}, {"term": "UPDATE", "definition": "Change values in matching rows."}, {"term": "DELETE", "definition": "Remove matching rows."}, {"term": "fetchone() / fetchall()", "definition": "Get one result row / get all remaining result rows."}]

121.title: Parameterized Queries and Preventing SQL Injection
121.learning_objectives: ["Put ? placeholders where SQL values belong.", "Send values separately from the SQL text.", "Explain how placeholders protect user input from SQL injection."]
121.prerequisites: Level 120: SQLite in Python: CRUD Operations
121.introduction: A search box may contain ordinary words or unexpected punctuation. A placeholder tells SQLite to treat what the person typed as data, not as another SQL instruction.
121.detailed_explanation:
A parameterized query has a question mark where a value should go. Python sends the SQL text and values separately: execute('SELECT role FROM users WHERE username = ?', (username,)).

The comma in (username,) makes a one-item tuple. If there are two question marks, provide two values in order. SQLite puts each value into its matching place safely.

Do not join user input into SQL text. A person could type punctuation that changes the query. With placeholders, that text stays a value to search for. Table and column names usually cannot use value placeholders, so choose those from trusted options.
121.terminology: [{"term": "Placeholder", "definition": "A ? mark that waits for a value."}, {"term": "Parameter", "definition": "A value sent separately to fill a placeholder."}, {"term": "SQL injection", "definition": "When input is mistakenly treated as part of a SQL instruction."}, {"term": "Tuple", "definition": "An ordered group of values, written in parentheses."}]

sql = 'SELECT role FROM users WHERE username = ?'
row = connection.execute(sql, (username,)).fetchone()

122.title: Version Control with Git and GitHub
122.learning_objectives: ["Describe what Git saves in a commit.", "Recognize a commit hash as an ID for a saved change.", "Explain what a branch is used for."]
122.introduction: Imagine saving a checkpoint in a game. If a new change causes trouble, the checkpoint helps you see what changed or return to an earlier version. Git does this for project files.
122.detailed_explanation:
Git is a tool that records selected changes to project files. Each saved checkpoint is a commit with a message and a long unique-looking ID called a hash. A short piece of the hash is often enough to recognize a commit in a list.

A branch is a named path of work. A team can keep stable work on main and try a new feature on another branch. When the feature is ready, people can review and combine it.

Git runs as a separate command-line tool. The Python examples here store and print sample Git information; they do not run Git commands or change your repository.

123.title: Debugging Python Code (pdb and Breakpoints)
123.learning_objectives: ["Explain how a debugger helps find a mistake.", "Recognize the pdb commands n, s, c, p, and q.", "Use a breakpoint to pause a program while debugging."]
123.prerequisites: Level 122: Version Control with Git and GitHub
123.introduction: A debugger is like a pause button for a program. You can stop at a line, look at values, and move through the program one step at a time.
123.detailed_explanation:
Python includes pdb, a debugger that can pause a running program. Put breakpoint() on a line to pause there. At the prompt, p name shows a value, n moves to the next line, s steps into a function, c continues, and q quits.

A debugger is helpful when the final answer is wrong and you need to see where a value changed. You can inspect it at the exact line where the program is running.

The boss challenge simulates a few pdb commands because this browser editor is not an interactive terminal. It lets you practice how commands change the current line and display a value without opening a separate prompt.
123.terminology: [{"term": "Debugger", "definition": "A tool that pauses code so you can inspect it."}, {"term": "Breakpoint", "definition": "A chosen place where the debugger pauses."}, {"term": "pdb", "definition": "Python's built-in interactive debugger."}, {"term": "Call stack", "definition": "The functions that led to the current line."}]
123.syntax_breakdown:
breakpoint()  # pause a real Python run here
# In the debugger:
# n     move to the next line
# p x   show x
# c     continue running

124.title: Automated Testing with unittest
124.learning_objectives: ["Explain why programs use repeatable tests.", "Put checks in a unittest.TestCase class.", "Use assertions to compare an answer with what you expected."]
124.introduction: After fixing one bug, you want to know you did not break something else. A test is a small automatic check you can run again whenever the code changes.
124.detailed_explanation:
A unit test checks one small behavior, such as one function. Python's unittest library gives you a TestCase class for grouping checks. Make a class based on TestCase, then write methods whose names start with test_.

An assertion checks a result. For example, assertEqual(actual, expected) passes when the two values match. If they do not, the test runner reports a failure.

A test runner finds and runs the test methods. Running the same checks after each change is faster and more reliable than trying every feature by hand. The small challenge uses assert directly; the boss uses a unittest suite.
124.terminology: [{"term": "Unit test", "definition": "A small automatic check of one behavior."}, {"term": "TestCase", "definition": "A unittest class that holds related test methods."}, {"term": "Assertion", "definition": "A check that passes when a condition is true."}, {"term": "Test runner", "definition": "The tool that finds and runs tests."}]

        self.assertEqual('foo'.upper(), 'FOO')
suite = unittest.TestLoader().loadTestsFromTestCase(TestStrings)
res = unittest.TextTestRunner(verbosity=0).run(suite)

125.title: Code Quality, PEP 8, and Type Hints
125.learning_objectives: ["Use PEP 8 names and spacing to make code easier to read.", "Add type hints to describe expected inputs and results.", "Explain that Python does not enforce ordinary hints by itself."]
125.introduction: A recipe is easier to follow when its steps are neat and its ingredients are labeled. PEP 8 is a shared style guide, and type hints label the kinds of values a function expects.
125.detailed_explanation:
PEP 8 is Python's common style guide. It recommends four spaces for indentation, lowercase_with_underscores for functions and variables, and CapitalizedWords for classes. Consistent style makes code easier to scan.

A type hint is a note in a function definition. In def area(width: float) -> float, the hint says width is expected to be a decimal number and the result is expected to be a decimal number. The arrow points to the result type.

Python normally does not reject a value just because it disagrees with a hint. Hints help readers, editors, and separate tools find possible mistakes. They are labels, not automatic conversions or safety checks.

def area(width: float, height: float) -> float:
    return width * height

126.title: World 12 Examination & Master Capstone: Complete Database Application
126.learning_objectives: ["Combine table creation, saved rows, and SELECT queries.", "Use placeholders when putting values into SQL.", "Explain how a larger project combines skills from earlier levels."]
126.introduction: A small school app might save students, find who qualifies for honors, and show a report. This level puts the database steps together from beginning to end.
126.detailed_explanation:
A database-backed program stores information in tables so it can be found later. The first example creates a table, inserts a row with question-mark placeholders, reads the row back, and closes the connection.

A larger student registry could also use functions, input checks, type hints, and tests. Each part has a job: the database saves records, functions organize actions, validation checks input, and tests catch mistakes.

The boss is a focused capstone. It saves three students, selects those whose GPA reaches the cutoff, sorts them, and prints a report. The cutoff is passed as a parameter so it stays data rather than SQL text. The practice database exists only in memory, so it leaves no files behind.
126.terminology: [{"term": "Capstone", "definition": "A final task that combines several skills."}, {"term": "Database", "definition": "An organized place to store and find records."}, {"term": "Transaction", "definition": "A group of database changes saved together."}, {"term": "Parameterized query", "definition": "SQL with placeholders and separate values."}]

connection = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
connection.execute('CREATE TABLE students (name TEXT, gpa REAL)')
connection.execute('INSERT INTO students VALUES (?, ?)', (name, gpa))
rows = connection.execute('SELECT name FROM students WHERE gpa >= ?', (cutoff,)).fetchall()
